concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Count and Recognize Numbers (1-20)
opening: Your child learns that counting is not just saying numbers in order. Each number matches exactly one real object. That one-to-one match is what makes comparing and adding possible later.
This clicks through repetition, not pressure. Count on the stairs and at snack time, not just at a table.
concepts.before: Your child should be able to say some numbers in order and recognize a few written numbers. If counting still feels inconsistent, slow down and count together using real objects before moving forward.
concepts.quickwin: Count each stair going up, then count backward coming down.
concepts.next: When your child counts objects accurately to 20 and recognizes numbers without guessing, they are ready for Concept 2: How to Teach Your Child to Compare Numbers and Quantities. That is where more, fewer and same start to click and prepare them for addition and subtraction.

acts.name: Stomp and Count
acts.desc: Stand in an open space and stomp or jump while counting out loud together. Count to 10, then keep going to 20. Change the movement each time you hit a new number. Kids remember numbers better when their whole body is involved.

acts.name: Number Song Round
acts.desc: Sing a counting song while doing something else, like washing hands or riding in the car. "One, Two, Buckle My Shoe" or a simple count-up chant works well. Singing the sequence locks in the order without any effort.

acts.name: Playdough Numbers
acts.desc: Roll playdough into snakes and shape them into numbers. Ask your child to build the number you call out, or name the one they made. No need for perfection. The rolling and pinching are part of the learning.

acts.name: Number Hunt Walk
acts.desc: Out for a walk or running errands? Numbers are everywhere. House numbers, mailboxes, menus, price tags, signs. Call out a number and ask your child to spot it, or point to a number and ask what comes before or after it. They will start pointing them out before you do.

acts.name: Snack Time Counting
acts.desc: Serving snacks? Count them before eating. Move them into a line, then a circle. Ask, "Did the number change when we moved them?" This is where kids start seeing that rearranging objects does not change how many there are.

acts.name: Chalk Number Town
acts.desc: Head outside and write numbers on the sidewalk with chalk. Call a number and have your child hop on it or stomp it out. Add arrows between numbers to show what comes next. If you don't have outdoor space, tape paper numbers on the floor indoors. Outdoor games make number recognition feel like play.

acts.name: Counting Collections
acts.desc: Cleaning up toys or sorting random things? Make a small pile and count together, touching one item at a time. Ask, "How can we keep track so we do not count the same one twice?" Before long your child will start organizing without being asked.

focused.name: Dot Card Match
focused.tool: Tiny Polka Dot by Math for Love
focused.desc: Spread out dot cards and numeral cards face up. Your child matches each quantity to the right numeral. Ask, "How did you know without counting?" The conversations that come out of this are where the real learning happens. Use this early in the concept when the hands-on matching is still building the one-to-one connection between quantities and numerals.

focused.name: Bead Count
focused.desc: Slide beads one at a time while counting aloud. Build small groups, then bigger ones. Point out that every row holds exactly ten beads. Once it clicks, your child will start doing this on their own just for fun. This is the mastery activity: sliding beads quickly and saying the next number before the bead slides over means number sequence is becoming automatic.

books.title: Chicka Chicka 1, 2, 3
books.author: Bill Martin Jr. and Michael Sampson

clicking.signs: Your child touches each object once as they count and stops on the right number. When you ask "How many?" they give you the last number they said, without counting again.
clicking.mixup: "There are 8!" when only 6 blocks are on the table, because two got counted twice. The words run faster than the finger, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Skip "count again." Give your child a cup. They drop each block in as they say its number. When the table is empty, the last number they said is the answer.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days counting small groups to 10 with real objects before moving on to 20.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Compare Numbers and Quantities
opening: Your child learns that numbers can tell you which group has more and which has fewer. When kids can say which pile has more and back it up with counting, they are ready to add and subtract.
Comparison shows up naturally when kids share snacks or line up toys. The goal is noticing first, counting to check second.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable counting small groups of objects, even if it is still a bit slow. Estimating and being wrong is part of the process.
concepts.quickwin: Put two uneven piles of crackers on the table and ask, "Which pile has more?" Count together to check.
concepts.next: When your child explains which group has more or fewer without needing a reminder and starts adjusting uneven piles on their own, they are ready for Concept 3: How to Teach Your Child Place Value (Tens and Ones). That is where numbers start to carry structure through tens and ones.

acts.name: Clap the Bigger Number
acts.desc: Call out two numbers. Your child claps the bigger one that many times. "Three or seven? Clap the bigger one." Swap roles and let your child call the numbers. Movement makes the comparison feel real instead of abstract.

acts.name: Tower Showdown
acts.desc: Build two block towers and stand them next to each other. Ask which one is taller and by how much. Before long your child will start adding blocks to even them up without being asked.

acts.name: More or Less Sort
acts.desc: Split a pile of small objects into two uneven groups. Ask which has more and which has fewer. Count to check. Kids love being right and love being surprised even more.

acts.name: Snack Math
acts.desc: Serving different snacks or portions? Ask, "Do you have more crackers or more grapes?" Count each group and then ask how many more one has than the other. Adjusting the piles to make them fair turns this into a real problem worth solving.

acts.name: Handful Guess
acts.desc: Grab a handful of small objects in each hand. Ask your child to guess which hand has more before counting. Open both hands and count to check. This builds estimation without any pressure to be right.

acts.name: Daily Spotter
acts.desc: Point out comparisons as you move through your day. "Which line is shorter at the store?" "Are there more red cars or blue ones?" Once kids start noticing, they will not stop.

acts.name: Nature Collection Compare
acts.desc: After being outside, sort a small collection of rocks or leaves into two groups. Line them up side by side and ask which group has more. Sorting the same objects a different way keeps it fresh.

focused.name: Balance Scale Challenge
focused.tool: Primary Balance Scale by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Place different numbers of small objects on each side of the scale. Ask which side is heavier and why. Adjust the objects until both sides balance. Watching the scale tip and settle makes the idea of equal feel real in a way words alone cannot. Use this early in the concept when the physical tipping is still making more and less visible.

focused.name: Ten Frame Compare
focused.desc: Fill two ten-frames with different amounts. Ask which has more and how your child knows. Count to check. Over time kids stop counting every dot and start reading the quantity at a glance. This is the mastery activity: naming which frame has more without counting each one means your child is reading quantity rather than tracking it.

clicking.signs: Your child points to the bigger pile and counts to check without being asked. They can tell you how many more one pile has, like "7 is 3 more than 4."
clicking.mixup: "This row has more!" when 5 spread-out buttons sit next to 7 bunched-up ones. Longer looks like more, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Skip "count them again." Pair the buttons up, one from each row side by side. The buttons left without a partner show which group has more.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days counting real objects one at a time (Grade 1, Concept 1) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Place Value (Tens and Ones)
opening: Your child learns that numbers are built by grouping ones into tens, and that where a digit sits tells you what it is worth. In 30, the 3 means three tens and the zero holds the ones place. Without this, two-digit numbers are just shapes. With it, addition and subtraction start to make sense.
Place value clicks when kids see it in real life repeatedly: through coins, snacks, bundled sticks and grouped objects.
concepts.before: Your child should be able to count objects and recognize numbers up to 20. If counting still feels uneven, spend more time there before introducing tens and ones.
concepts.quickwin: Count out 10 snacks, put them in a small cup, and call it "one ten." Add a few more to the side and say the number together.
concepts.next: When your child groups objects into tens on their own and describes two-digit numbers using tens and ones without prompting, they are ready for Concept 4: How to Teach Your Child Addition Within 10. That is where these groups get combined to solve addition problems.

acts.name: Jumping Tens
acts.desc: Count to 20 while jumping. Jump once for each number. When you hit 10, clap loud and shout "One ten!" Keep jumping to 20 and shout "Two tens!" Your child feels the rhythm of tens without thinking about it.

acts.name: Snack Pack Tens
acts.desc: Pour snacks onto the table and count ten into a cup. That cup is one ten. Keep going until you cannot make another full group. Count the full cups first, then the extras. "Two tens and four ones makes 24." Snacks get portioned and math gets done at the same time.

acts.name: Zero Hunt
acts.desc: Out running errands? Start noticing zeros on prices and house numbers. Ask, "What would that number be without the zero?" Kids quickly see that zero changes the value of a number, not just how it looks.

acts.name: Bundling Station
acts.desc: Sorting pencils or straws? Bundle every ten together with a rubber band. Count bundles first, then leftovers. Counting by tens is faster and kids notice this right away.

acts.name: Coin Trade Game
acts.desc: Dump out pennies and count ten together. Trade them for a dime. Say it out loud: "Ten ones became one ten." Keep trading until you run out. Trading makes place value feel like a rule that actually makes sense.

acts.name: Playdough Tens and Ones
acts.desc: Roll ten small playdough balls, press them into one long snake. The snake is "one ten." Roll a few extra balls for the ones. Name the number you built. Your child sees the transformation from many small pieces to one group.

acts.name: Number Spot on the Walk
acts.desc: Point to numbers you pass on a walk. Ask, "How many tens does that number have? How many ones?" Keep it quick and casual. This is not a quiz, just noticing. If you don't have a walk nearby, do the same with numbers on food packaging or price tags at home.

focused.name: Place Value Build
focused.desc: Say a number like 23. Your child builds it with two ten rods and three unit cubes. Count by tens then by ones. Build a number wrong on purpose and let your child catch the mistake. Catching errors builds understanding faster than getting things right every time. Use this early in the concept when the physical blocks are still making the value of each place visible.

focused.name: Tens and Ones Sort
focused.tool: Place Value Frame with Base Ten Blocks by hand2mind
focused.desc: Say a number and have your child place the blocks into the correct compartments of the frame, ones in the ones slot and tens in the tens slot. Read the number together. Then build a second number and ask which one has more tens. This is the mastery activity: reading and building any two-digit number quickly without counting individual units means tens and ones are understood as places, not just piles.

books.title: Sir Cumference and All the King's Tens
books.author: Cindy Neuschwander

tools.name: Place Value Frame with Base Ten Blocks

clicking.signs: Your child builds 34 with 3 tens and 4 ones without counting every piece. They can tell you the 3 in 34 means 30, not 3.
clicking.mixup: Writing fifteen as 51. The word fifteen says the 5 first, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build it. Make one bundle of ten sticks and set 5 loose sticks beside it. Ask, "Which do we write first, the bundle or the loose ones?" Write 1 under the bundle and 5 under the loose sticks.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days counting and reading numbers to 20 (Grade 1, Concept 1) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Addition Within 10
opening: Your child learns that addition is about putting groups together and finding how many there are in all. This turns counting into combining and builds the foundation for mental math and word problems.
Addition shows up naturally when kids put toys together or combine snacks. Help them see it as something they already do.
concepts.before: Your child should be able to count objects up to 10 and recognize small quantities without counting every time. If counting is still unsteady, spend more time there first.
concepts.quickwin: Put three crackers on one side of a plate and two on the other. Push them together and count how many there are in all.
concepts.next: When your child combines groups and gives you the total without counting every object, they are ready for Concept 5: How to Teach Your Child Subtraction Within 10. That is where they learn what happens when part of a group is taken away.

acts.name: Jump and Add
acts.desc: Stand a few feet apart and take turns calling out two small numbers. Your child jumps the first number, pauses, then jumps the second. Count all the jumps together. Bodies make addition concrete before numbers on paper ever could.

acts.name: Addition Chant
acts.desc: Make up a simple beat and chant additions together. "Two and three is five. Four and one is five." Clap on each number. Do this in the car or while walking. The rhythm locks in facts that drills never seem to.

acts.name: Snack Combiner
acts.desc: Put some snacks on one side of the plate and some on the other. Ask, "You have three here and two there. How many altogether?" Push them together and count. Eating the answer is a solid motivator.

acts.name: Toy Join-Up
acts.desc: Cleaning up? Count the toys on the rug, then the ones on the shelf. "Let's put them together. How many now?" Cleanup becomes a math problem worth solving.

acts.name: Playdough Number Scenes
acts.desc: Your child sculpts a small scene with playdough animals or shapes. "You made four ducks and two frogs. How many creatures are there?" Then let your child make up a question for you. Making up their own problems is more powerful than answering yours.

acts.name: Laundry Add-On
acts.desc: Folding clothes? Count four socks in one pile and add three more. "We had four, we added three. How many now?" Boring chores become slightly less boring.

acts.name: Puddle or Leaf Add-Up
acts.desc: Outside? Collect leaves or rocks in two small piles. Combine them and count the total. Let your child rearrange the piles and check if the total changes. It never does, and that surprises them every time. If you don't have outdoor space, use small objects on the kitchen table.

focused.name: Counter Combos
focused.desc: Start with one small group of counters, then slide over another. Count the total. Say it out loud: "Four and three makes seven." Keep the two colors separate so your child can still see both parts inside the whole. Use this early in the concept when the visible separation of two groups is still making the combining step concrete.

focused.name: Ten Frame Additions
focused.desc: Fill part of a ten-frame, then add more counters. Ask how many spaces are filled now. Seeing the frame fill up helps kids understand totals without recounting everything from scratch. This is the mastery activity: adding to a partially filled frame and naming the total without counting every dot means addition is becoming something your child can visualize.

clicking.signs: Your child starts at the bigger number and counts on: "5... 6, 7, 8." They can show 3 + 4 with two groups of objects and tell you the total.
clicking.mixup: "3 + 4 is 6," because they said 3 again when they started counting on. Starting on the wrong number is easy, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Hide 3 crackers under a cup and say "three." The cup holds the three, so the first cracker your child touches is "four." Count the rest from there: "four, five, six, seven." Lift the cup and count everything to check.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days counting small groups with real objects (Grade 1, Concept 1) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Subtraction Within 10
opening: Your child learns that subtraction starts with a group and shows what is left after some are taken away. This understanding connects directly to addition and to problem solving with bigger numbers later on.
Subtraction shows up naturally when snacks get eaten or toys get put away. The goal is helping your child see it as part of everyday life, not a separate rule to memorize.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable counting to 10 and combining small groups. If addition still feels unsteady, spend a little more time there first.
concepts.quickwin: Put six grapes on a plate. Eat two together and count how many are left.
concepts.next: When your child can tell you how many are left without recounting every object, they are ready for Concept 6: How to Teach Your Child to Make 10. That is where addition and subtraction start working together around the number 10.

acts.name: Step It Back
acts.desc: Take five steps forward, counting each one. Then step back one at a time while counting down. "You were on five, now you're on four, now three." The whole body tracking backward makes subtraction feel like something real, not just a symbol on a page.

acts.name: Five Little Monkeys Clap-Along
acts.desc: Sing "Five Little Monkeys Jumping on the Bed" and hold up fingers for each monkey. Fold one finger down and clap once each time a monkey falls off. Kids ask to do this again before the song is even over.

acts.name: Snack Takeaway
acts.desc: Start with a small pile of snacks. Count them together. Eat one or two and count what is left. "You had six, you ate two. How many are there now?" Watching the pile shrink makes subtraction obvious.

acts.name: Toy Clean-Up Math
acts.desc: Count how many toys are on the floor. Put a few away. "We started with eight, we put away three. How many are still out?" Cleanup has a purpose now.

acts.name: Finger Fold Down
acts.desc: Hold up a number of fingers. Fold one down at a time. "We had seven fingers up. One went down. How many are up now?" Easy to do anywhere and impossible to lose the materials.

acts.name: Playdough Take-Away
acts.desc: Make a small group of playdough balls together. Squash a few with a dramatic "pop." Count what is left. Your child will want to be the one doing the squashing.

acts.name: Nature Pile Takeaway
acts.desc: Outside? Build a small pile of rocks or sticks. Remove some and count what remains. Switch who removes and who counts. Working with objects from nature keeps it from feeling like a lesson. If you don't have outdoor space, use small objects on the kitchen table.

focused.name: Cube Break Apart
focused.desc: Build a small cube train. Break off a section and set it aside. Count what remains. Use two colors to show what stayed and what was taken away. The snap gives a satisfying physical moment to the act of subtracting. Use this early in the concept when the physical breaking is still making the take-away step visible.

focused.name: Subtraction Stories
focused.desc: Make up a quick story. "Seven frogs were on a log. Three jumped off." Your child moves three counters to the side and counts what is left. Making the story together is even better than you telling it. This is the mastery activity: moving counters and naming the answer before counting every one means subtraction is becoming something your child can picture.

books.title: Five Little Monkeys Jumping on the Bed
books.author: Eileen Christelow

tools.name: Cloud Hoppers Addition and Subtraction Game

clicking.signs: Your child starts with the whole group, takes some away and tells you what is left without recounting from one. They can tell a quick story that matches 7 − 2.
clicking.mixup: "5 − 3 is 8." Two numbers side by side often mean put them together, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Act it out with snacks. Put 5 on the plate, eat 3 and ask, "Do we have more or fewer now?" Once your child sees the pile shrink, a bigger answer stops making sense.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on putting groups together (Grade 1, Concept 4) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Make 10
opening: Your child learns that numbers can be broken apart and put back together to make 10. This makes addition and subtraction faster and sets up mental math strategies that last all the way through grade school.
Making 10 becomes automatic through daily exposure, not drilling. Help your child bump into it often and they will start doing it without thinking.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable counting to 10 and adding small groups. If addition within 10 still feels shaky, spend more time there first.
concepts.quickwin: Hold up six fingers and ask, "How many more fingers do we need to make 10?" Raise them together and count.
concepts.next: When your child answers "how many more to make 10" without counting every time, they are ready for Concept 7: How to Teach Your Child Shapes (Identifying, Attributes, and Building). That is where shapes and spatial thinking enter the picture.

acts.name: Make 10 Freeze Dance
acts.desc: Play music and freeze when it stops. While you are both frozen, hold up some fingers and ask your child how many more make 10. Start the music again and keep going. The game makes the math feel urgent and fun at the same time.

acts.name: Make 10 Song
acts.desc: Chant or sing the pairs that make 10 to any simple beat. "One and nine, two and eight, three and seven, four and six, five and five." Repeat it in the car or at the table while doing something else. The rhythm does the memorizing for you.

acts.name: Snack to Ten
acts.desc: Put some snacks on the plate and ask, "How many more do we need to make 10?" Add pieces one at a time and count together. Finishing the set feels genuinely satisfying to kids.

acts.name: Toy Fill-Up
acts.desc: Line up toys and stop before reaching 10. "We have seven cars. How many more do we need to make 10?" Let your child grab the missing ones and check. Then rearrange and do it again with a different starting number.

acts.name: Playdough Pairs
acts.desc: Roll 10 small balls in two colors. Make a row of 1 red and 9 blue, then 2 red and 8 blue, and keep going. Line the rows up and look at the pattern. Your child will notice something is happening before you say a word about it.

acts.name: Hidden Stones
acts.desc: Outside, lay 10 small stones in a row and count them together. While your child looks away, hide some under a flowerpot. Your child counts the stones still showing and tells you how many are hidden. Lift the pot to check. If you don't have outdoor space, use buttons under a cup on the table.

acts.name: Bedtime Make 10 Talk
acts.desc: Call out numbers while brushing teeth or getting ready for bed. "If I have 4, how many more to make 10?" Keep it light and quick. No materials needed. This is the one that sticks because it happens every single night.

focused.name: Ten Frame Fill
focused.desc: Fill part of a ten-frame and ask how many empty spaces remain. Slide counters in to complete it. Say it out loud: "Seven needs three more to make 10." Let your child fill the frame and announce the pair. Use this early in the concept when seeing the empty spaces is still making the missing amount obvious.

focused.name: Counter Pairs
focused.desc: Build combinations that make 10 using two different colors. Show that 6 and 4, 8 and 2, and 5 and 5 all reach the same total. Switch which color goes first. Kids quickly notice that the order of the colors does not change the sum. This is the mastery activity: building different pairs quickly and naming each one without counting means making 10 is becoming a reflex.

clicking.signs: Your child holds up 7 fingers and says "3 more" without counting. They can name a few pairs that make 10, like 6 and 4 or 8 and 2.
clicking.mixup: "6 needs 5 more to make 10." Your child counted "6, 7, 8, 9, 10" on their fingers, but the 6 was already there. Counting the starting number is easy to do, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Fill 6 spaces of a ten-frame or a 10-cup egg carton. Ask your child to count only the empty spaces. The empty spaces are the answer.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on counting on in addition (Grade 1, Concept 4) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Shapes (Identifying, Attributes, and Building)
opening: Your child learns to name shapes, describe what makes each one different and figure out how shapes combine. This builds the spatial reasoning that supports fractions and later geometry work.
Shapes already live in your home and your child's play. The goal is noticing them and building with them.
concepts.before: Your child should recognize a few basic shapes like circle, square and triangle. If shape names are still brand new, focus on spotting and naming before talking about sides and corners.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child to find three shapes in one room. Name each one together.
concepts.next: When your child names shapes on their own and uses words like sides, corners, flat and round, they are ready for Concept 8: How to Teach Your Child to Compare and Measure Length. That is where size and distance start to matter.

acts.name: Shape Dance Freeze
acts.desc: Play music and when it stops, call out a shape. Your child makes that shape with their body. Hands pressed together over the head make a triangle. Curling up tight makes a circle. Laughter is part of it.

acts.name: Shape Song Build-Up
acts.desc: Sing a shape chant together. "A triangle has three sides, three sides, three sides. A triangle has three sides and three corners too." Make up verses for each shape. The sillier the tune, the better it sticks.

acts.name: Shape Spotter Walk
acts.desc: Walking through the house or neighborhood? Call out shapes as you see them. "That window is a rectangle. That manhole cover is a circle." Kids will start pointing them out before you finish the sentence.

acts.name: Snack Shape Check
acts.desc: Before eating, look at the food. Crackers and sandwich halves come in lots of shapes. "Which ones are rectangles? Which have no straight sides?" Snack time slows down just enough to notice things.

acts.name: Playdough Shape Build
acts.desc: Roll and press playdough into shapes. Count the sides. Press two triangles together along one side and ask what shape appears. Your child is doing geometry while thinking they are just playing.

acts.name: Art Table Shapes
acts.desc: Challenge your child to make a picture using only certain shapes. "Can you make an animal using circles and triangles?" Creativity does the heavy lifting here.

acts.name: Chalk Shape Town
acts.desc: Outside with chalk? Draw shapes of different sizes on the sidewalk. Jump in the circles and walk along the edges of the rectangles. Ask your child to count the corners of each shape they land on. If you don't have outdoor space, cut shapes from paper and arrange them on the floor.

focused.name: Pattern Block Builds
focused.desc: Build pictures with pattern blocks. Count sides and corners on each piece. Combine two shapes and ask what new shape appears. Let your child explain what they notice before you say anything. Use this early in the concept when the physical fitting and combining is still making shape relationships visible.

focused.name: Geoboard Shapes
focused.desc: Stretch rubber bands to make shapes on the geoboard. Count the corners and sides. Move one corner of a band to a new peg and ask what changed. Shapes start to feel flexible instead of fixed. This is the mastery activity: building a shape from a verbal description and naming its properties without prompting means shape understanding is solid.

books.title: My Very First Book of Shapes
books.author: Eric Carle

books.title: Captain Invincible and the Space Shapes
books.author: Stuart J. Murphy

clicking.signs: Your child calls a tilted square a square, not a diamond. They count sides and corners to explain why a shape is a triangle.
clicking.mixup: "That's not a triangle, it's upside down." Most triangles in books sit flat on one side, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Cut a triangle from paper. Turn it slowly and ask, "Did it change? Count the sides again." Three sides and three corners make a triangle, whichever way it points.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days spotting and naming shapes around the house before counting sides and corners.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Compare and Measure Length
opening: Your child learns to compare objects by length, decide which is longer or shorter, and measure with the same small object over and over, like paper clips. This connects to addition now and to rulers later on.
Length shows up naturally when kids line things up or notice that one thing is bigger. Compare first, then measure.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable comparing quantities and counting small groups. If ideas like more and fewer are still shaky, spend time on Concept 2 before moving here.
concepts.quickwin: Find two objects in the room. Line them up at one end and ask which one is longer.
concepts.next: When your child lines things up before comparing and chooses a measuring unit without being told, they are ready for Concept 9: How to Teach Your Child to Tell Time (Hour and Half-Hour). That is where numbers are used to track time and daily routines.

acts.name: Body Measure Walk
acts.desc: Waiting somewhere or heading to the car? Measure things with your body. "How many of your feet long is the couch?" "Is the doorway wider than your arm span?" Kids love using themselves as the measuring tool.

acts.name: Length Freeze Dance
acts.desc: Play music and when it stops, your child grabs two small things nearby, like a spoon and a sock. They line them up at one end and tell you which is longer. Then the music starts again. Freezing and checking keeps it feeling like a game instead of a lesson.

acts.name: Line It Up
acts.desc: Comparing toys or books? Line them up side by side on the floor starting from the same end. "Which one is longer? Which is shorter?" Lining things up removes guessing and makes the answer visible.

acts.name: Block Length Test
acts.desc: Building with blocks? Lay them end to end instead of stacking. "How many blocks long is your train?" "Is your bridge longer than mine?" Building becomes measuring without anyone calling it that.

acts.name: Snack Stick Compare
acts.desc: Eating pretzels or carrot sticks? Hold two up and compare. "Which one is longer?" "Can you find two that are the same length?" Snack decisions get very thoughtful.

acts.name: Playdough Snakes
acts.desc: Roll two playdough snakes and ask which one is longer. Roll them out more or squish them shorter and check again. Your child discovers that length changes when you stretch or squish, and stays the same if you only move it to a new spot.

acts.name: Clean-Up Sort by Length
acts.desc: Putting things away? Sort items by length before storing them. "Longest ones here, shortest ones there." Cleanup gets a purpose and goes faster.

focused.name: Rod Comparisons
focused.desc: Lay rods side by side and compare lengths. Order them shortest to longest. Combine smaller rods to match the length of a longer one. The colors make length relationships easy to see without counting every unit. Use this early in the concept when side-by-side comparison is still the main strategy.

focused.name: Cube Measuring
focused.desc: Build cube trains and use them to measure objects around the room. "This book is five cubes long." Measure two objects and compare the results. Using the same unit is what makes comparisons fair. This is the mastery activity: choosing a unit, measuring two objects, and comparing the numbers means length measurement is understood as a consistent system.

books.title: Me and the Measure of Things
books.author: Joan Sweeney

clicking.signs: Your child lines up the ends of two objects before saying which is longer. They measure with cubes or paper clips and leave no gaps between them.
clicking.mixup: "The pencil is longer," when its end only sticks out further because it starts further along the table. Where something ends looks like how long it is, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Slide both objects so their ends touch the same edge of the table. Then ask again. Make "line up the ends" the first move every time.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days comparing groups side by side (Grade 1, Concept 2) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Tell Time (Hour and Half-Hour)
opening: Your child learns to read the clock at the hour and half-hour and connect those times to real moments in the day. Time becomes meaningful when it is tied to meals and bedtime, not just to a clock face on a worksheet.
This builds independence and sets the foundation for working out how long things take later on.
concepts.before: Your child should recognize numbers 1 through 12 and understand parts of the day like morning and night. If number recognition is still shaky, revisit that first.
concepts.quickwin: Point to a clock and say the time out loud. Ask your child to say it back.
concepts.next: When your child reads hour and half-hour times without hesitation and connects them to real events in the day, they are ready for Concept 10: How to Teach Your Child to Sort and Organize Data. That is where they begin collecting, grouping and making sense of information.

acts.name: Clock Hop Game
acts.desc: Tape a big clock face on the floor or draw one with chalk outside. Your child stands in the middle and becomes the hour hand, turning their body to point at the number you call. "Show me 4 o'clock!" You stand beside them as the minute hand, arm pointing at 12 or 6. Kids love being the clock.

acts.name: Schedule Talk
acts.desc: Going through your day? Name the time out loud whenever something happens. "We eat lunch at 12 o'clock. Bath starts at 6:30." Hearing time connected to real moments is what makes clocks feel useful.

acts.name: Half Hour Song
acts.desc: Make up a simple chant for hours and half hours. "The big hand on the 12 means o'clock. The big hand on the 6 means half past." Sing it a few times throughout the day. The repetition is the whole point.

acts.name: Match the Clock
acts.desc: Draw a simple clock face. Call out a time and ask your child to draw where the hands go. Flip it around: draw the hands and ask what time it shows. No materials needed beyond paper and a pencil.

acts.name: Movement by the Hour
acts.desc: Set a clock to a certain hour and move that many times. Jump three times for 3 o'clock. Clap six times for 6 o'clock. For half past, add one big spin at the end. Bodies make time stick.

acts.name: Half-Hour Spotting
acts.desc: Any time the big hand hits the 6, call it out. "Half past!" Ask where the little hand is pointing. This builds half-hour awareness without stopping what you are doing.

acts.name: Pretend Schedule Play
acts.desc: Play house or school and build a schedule. "School starts at 8 o'clock. Recess is at 10:30." Set a toy clock to match each event. Pretend play makes kids care about telling time before it ever feels like a lesson.

focused.name: Hands-On Clock Play
focused.desc: Move the hour hand to different positions and name each time. Add the minute hand at 12 for full hours and at 6 for half hours. Say the time out loud each time. Then switch roles and let your child set the time for you. Use this early in the concept when the physical hands are still reinforcing how the hour and minute hands relate.

focused.name: Routine Matching
focused.tool: Turn and Tell Wooden Clock by Melissa and Doug
focused.desc: Match clock times to real daily activities. Set the clock for breakfast or bedtime. Watch the digital window change as the hands move. Connecting analog and digital formats helps both make sense. This is the mastery activity: setting the clock to a time you describe and reading back a time you set means your child understands the clock rather than just mimicking hand positions.

books.title: Telling Time with Big Mama Cat
books.author: Dan Harper

books.title: What Time Is It, Mr. Crocodile?
books.author: Judy Sierra

clicking.signs: Your child reads 3:00 and 3:30 on a clock face and tells you what happens at that time of day. They know the little hand tells the hour.
clicking.mixup: Reading 6:00 as 12:30 by mixing up the hands. Both hands point at numbers, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Name the hands out loud: the little hand tells the hour. Have your child find the little hand first and say its number before looking at the big hand.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days reading the numbers 1 to 12 around the clock face (Grade 1, Concept 1) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Sort and Organize Data
opening: Your child learns to sort objects into groups and count each group so the results are easy to compare. Data shows up naturally when kids sort toys or ask which option has more.
The goal is collecting information with a purpose and using it to answer a real question.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable counting small groups and comparing quantities. If more, fewer and same are still shaky, spend time on Concept 2 before moving here.
concepts.quickwin: Sort the objects on the kitchen table into two groups. Count each one and say which has more.
concepts.next: This completes the Grade 1 math core. Your child is ready to carry these ideas into Grade 2, where the numbers get bigger and the foundation you built together does the heavy lifting.

acts.name: Sort and Stomp
acts.desc: Put a mixed pile of objects on the floor. Call out a group, like "something red," and your child runs to find one that fits, stomping back to drop it in the right group. Keep going until the pile is sorted. Movement and sorting together make this surprisingly gripping for first graders.

acts.name: Snack Survey
acts.desc: Offering snack choices? Ask everyone at home to pick one. Make a tally mark for each choice. Count the marks and decide which wins. Decisions feel fair when data is involved.

acts.name: Toy Sort and Count
acts.desc: Sorting toys during cleanup? Sort by type first: cars in one pile, animals in another. Count each pile and compare. Cleanup has a plan and goes faster.

acts.name: Cereal Color Count
acts.desc: Pour a small bowl of colorful cereal. Sort by color and count each group. Ask which color showed up most and which showed up least. Breakfast gets very intentional.

acts.name: Favorite Anything Poll
acts.desc: Waiting around? Run a quick poll. Favorite color or favorite animal. Keep tallies on paper or fingers. Compare results and talk about what surprised you. Kids love discovering that their answer was not the most popular one.

acts.name: Nature Collection Sort
acts.desc: Back from outside? Sort rocks or leaves by size or type. Line each group up and count. Ask which group has the most. Sorting the same objects a different way the next day keeps the activity from getting old.

acts.name: Weather Tally Chart
acts.desc: Keep a simple tally chart of the weather each day for a week. At the end, count each category and compare. Your child decides how to group the days. Choosing the categories is half the learning.

focused.name: Bear Graph
focused.tool: Three Bear Family Counters by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Pour out a handful of bears. Your child sorts them by color, then lines each color up in its own row from the same starting edge. Ask, "Which row is longest? How many more red bears than blue?" Lining the rows up makes the answer visible before anyone counts. Use this early in the concept when the length of each row is still doing the comparing.

focused.name: Cube Graph Build
focused.desc: Ask a question, like each family member's favorite fruit. Stack one cube for each answer, one tower per fruit. Compare column heights and count totals. Pull the cubes apart and rebuild to double-check. This is the mastery activity: building a graph independently and using it to answer a comparison question means your child understands what graphs are for, not just how to build them.

clicking.signs: Your child sorts a pile into groups without help and tells you which group has the most. They answer "how many more?" by looking at the tally or the cube tower.
clicking.mixup: "Blue has the most," because the blue bears are spread out over more space. More space looks like more bears, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Line each color up in its own row from the same starting edge, one bear per space. Ask which row is longest, then count to check.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on comparing groups (Grade 1, Concept 2) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Skip Counting and Number Patterns
opening: Skip counting is how your child stops counting one by one and starts moving through numbers with confidence. It builds the mental number line they will rely on for multiplication and mental math for years to come.
concepts.before: Your child should be able to count to 100 by ones without losing track. If that feels shaky, spend a week counting together on the stairs and at snack time before moving forward. Skip counting only makes sense once the ones underneath it are solid.
concepts.quickwin: Count to 20 by 2s together right now, clapping on each number.
concepts.next: When your child can skip count by 2s and 5s without losing track, then count by 10s to 100, they are ready for Concept 2: How to Teach Your Child Place Value to Hundreds. Counting by 10s is exactly what makes hundreds click.

acts.name: Move and Count
acts.desc: Pick a skip counting pattern, like 2s or 5s, and move through it together. Whisper the numbers in between and jump only on the numbers in the pattern. For 2s: whisper "1," jump and say "2," whisper "3," jump and say "4." The quiet numbers make the gaps real. Switch to clapping or hopping to keep it fresh.

acts.name: Staircase Skip Counting
acts.desc: Heading up the stairs? Count by 2s or 10s, one number per step. Keep the same pattern coming down. If your child loses track, pause and work out the next number together before moving on. The pattern has to hold across the whole flight, which is what makes this one work.

acts.name: Number Pattern Art
acts.desc: Draw a number line from 0 to 30 on a long strip of paper. Have your child color every 2nd number one color and every 5th number another. Stand back and ask, "What do you notice?" That is the only question you need. The pattern they see is the one they remember.

acts.name: Mystery Pattern Game
acts.desc: Write a skip counting pattern on small slips of paper, one number per slip, and leave two numbers blank. Lay them out in a row. Ask, "Can you figure out what's missing?" Once your child fills the gaps, mix them up and try a different skip. If writing feels slow, use coins or blocks to mark each spot.

acts.name: Nickel Store
acts.desc: Set up a pretend store where every price is a multiple of 5, like 10, 15, 20 and 25 cents. Pay with real nickels. Each nickel is 5, so your child pays by counting nickels in 5s instead of one by one. The store gives skip counting a real reason to exist.

acts.name: Kitchen Skip Counting
acts.desc: Setting the table or sorting forks? Count by 2s instead of ones. "We need forks for 4 people. Count them out by 2s." Socks in pairs work the same way. No extra prep needed.

acts.name: Sidewalk Skip Patterns
acts.desc: Outside with chalk? Draw a long number line on the driveway from 0 to 30. Circle only the numbers in one pattern, so for 5s you circle 5, 10, 15, 20 and so on. Your child hops from circle to circle, saying each number. The numbers they hop over are the gaps they are skipping. If you don't have outdoor space, use masking tape on the floor indoors.

focused.name: Bead Skip Counting
focused.desc: Slide beads over in groups that match your skip count: two at a time for 2s, five at a time for 5s. Say the total as each group lands. Once the pattern feels steady, cover the beads already moved with your hand and ask your child to say the next number before sliding. This slows down automatic chanting and builds real understanding. Use this early in the concept when the hands-on grouping is still making each jump visible.

focused.name: Hundred Chart Patterns
focused.tool: Hundred Pocket Chart by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Start at 2 and count by 2s, flipping each card you land on to its colored side. Step back and look at the columns the colors fall in. Then try 5s. Ask, "What pattern do you see? Does counting by 10s always land in the same column?" Let your child choose the next pattern. This is the mastery activity: spotting and describing the pattern on the chart means skip counting is becoming structure rather than a memorized chant.

books.title: How Many Feet in the Bed?
books.author: Diane Johnston Hamm

clicking.signs: Your child counts by 5s from 5 to 50 without dropping back to ones. They can start in the middle, like "35, 40, 45," without going back to the beginning.
clicking.mixup: Counting by 2s as "2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 11, 12." Once the chant runs out, counting by ones takes over, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Go back to objects. Line up socks in pairs and touch each pair as you count: "2, 4, 6." Stop at 10 and ask, "How many socks are in the next pair?" Then keep going together.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days grouping real objects into tens (Grade 1, Concept 3) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Place Value to Hundreds
opening: Place value is the system behind every number your child will work with. When they understand that the position of a digit tells you its value, reading and comparing numbers stops being guesswork.
In 352, the 3 means three hundreds, the 5 means five tens and the 2 means two ones.
concepts.before: Your child should read numbers to 100 and show any two-digit number as tens and ones. If tens feel shaky, spend a few days bundling household objects into groups of ten (Grade 1, Concept 3). Hundreds are just ten tens, so the tens have to be solid first.
concepts.quickwin: Grab 13 small objects, like pennies or blocks. Ask your child to make a pile of ten and count what's left. Say together: "1 ten and 3 ones. That's 13."
concepts.next: When your child can build and compare three-digit numbers and explain what each digit is worth, they are ready for Concept 3: How to Teach Your Child Two-Digit Addition and Subtraction. Place value is what makes adding bigger numbers make sense instead of feeling like memorized steps.

acts.name: Number of the Day Walk
acts.desc: On your next walk, pick a three-digit number, like 134. Say it out loud and walk it together: 1 giant step for the hundred, 3 hops for the tens and 4 small steps for the ones. Pick a new number at each corner. Your child starts to feel that bigger places carry more weight.

acts.name: Staircase Hundreds
acts.desc: Heading upstairs? Each stair is worth ten. Count 10, 20, 30 as you climb. When you reach 100, stop and say, "Ten tens make one hundred." Keep going past 100 if you have more stairs: 110, 120. Short trips make this a daily habit with no setup.

acts.name: Place Value Art
acts.desc: Draw three large boxes side by side and label them H, T and O. Call out a number and have your child draw marks in each box: a big square for each hundred, a line for each ten and a dot for each one. When finished, they read the number back. Hang a few on the wall and point to them when numbers come up in conversation.

acts.name: Digit Detective
acts.desc: Your child is a detective. Write a three-digit number on paper and ask them to crack the code: how many hundreds, how many tens and how many ones are hiding inside? Make a wrong guess on purpose so they get to correct you. Then switch roles and let them write the mystery number for you.

acts.name: Build-a-Number
acts.desc: Set out three cups labeled hundreds, tens and ones, plus a pile of dried beans. Agree that a bean in the hundreds cup is worth 100 and a bean in the tens cup is worth 10. Call out a number and have your child fill the cups to match. Then fill the cups yourself and ask them to read the number. Swap roles so they get to call out numbers too.

acts.name: Receipt Reading
acts.desc: Pull out a grocery receipt and find a price like $2.47. Cover the dollar sign and the dot with your finger so it reads 247. Ask, "Which digit tells the hundreds? Which tells the ones?" Receipts give place value a real reason to matter.

acts.name: Sidewalk Number Builder
acts.desc: Outside with chalk? Draw three large boxes on the driveway labeled hundreds, tens and ones. Call out a number and have your child write each digit in the right box. Then they read it back and tell you what each digit is worth. Build five numbers together. If you don't have outdoor space, use large paper on the floor indoors.

focused.name: Base Ten Block Building
focused.desc: Call out a three-digit number and have your child build it using flats for hundreds, rods for tens and units for ones. Once built, ask, "Can you make the same number a different way?" Trading 10 rods for 1 flat, or the reverse, is where understanding shows up. Don't rush the trade. Use this early in the concept when the hands-on trading is still making the value of each place visible.

focused.name: Place Value Showdown
focused.desc: Remove the face cards. Aces count as 1 and 10s count as zero. Each of you draws three cards, one at a time. After each draw, decide whether that digit goes in your hundreds, tens or ones place, and it can't move later. Read both numbers aloud and compare. This is the mastery activity: deciding where a digit goes before seeing the next card means your child understands that position decides value.

books.title: Sir Cumference and All the King's Tens
books.author: Cindy Neuschwander

clicking.signs: Your child reads 305 as "three hundred five" and builds it with no rods at all. They can tell you the 4 in 247 is worth 40.
clicking.mixup: Writing three hundred five as 3005. They write what they hear, 300 and then 5, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build it with blocks first: 3 flats, no rods, 5 units. Then draw three boxes for hundreds, tens and ones and write one digit per box. The empty tens box gets a zero.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on tens and ones (Grade 1, Concept 3) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Two-Digit Addition and Subtraction
opening: Two-digit addition and subtraction is where place value stops being an idea and becomes a tool. When your child understands that tens add to tens and ones add to ones, they can work with bigger numbers without losing track or leaning on memorized steps.
concepts.before: Your child should add and subtract within 10 with confidence and know that a two-digit number is made of tens and ones. If either feels shaky, spend a few days on Concept 2 or on making 10 (Grade 1, Concept 6) first. Regrouping is just making a ten, done with bigger numbers.
concepts.quickwin: Put 23 small objects on the table. Ask your child to add 10 more. Count the new total together and ask, "What changed? What stayed the same?"
concepts.next: When your child can add and subtract two-digit numbers and explain what happens when ones need to be regrouped, they are ready for Concept 4: How to Teach Your Child Multiplication with Equal Groups and Arrays. The grouping thinking they built here is what multiplication runs on.

acts.name: Jump the Number Line
acts.desc: Tape a number line on the floor with masking tape and mark every 10 from 0 to 100. Call out a starting number and an amount to add or subtract. Your child jumps by tens first, then steps by ones. "Start at 34. Add 20. Where do you land?" Jumping across the tens makes them concrete.

acts.name: Staircase Addition
acts.desc: Heading upstairs? Pick a starting number at the bottom, like 14. Add 10 for every step you climb: "14, 24, 34, 44." Coming down, take away 10 per step. Your child sees that only the tens digit changes.

acts.name: Number Story Drawing
acts.desc: Your child draws a simple scene, like a basket of apples. Give them a starting number and an amount to add or take away: "You had 32 apples. You picked 15 more. Draw it." They draw the change and write the number sentence underneath. The drawing slows them down enough to think about what is actually happening.

acts.name: The Banker Game
acts.desc: Your child is the bank. Bring them handfuls of pennies. Every time you have 10 pennies, they trade them for a dime. Keep going until you need several trades. Handing over 10 and getting 1 back makes the trade feel real.

acts.name: Build and Combine
acts.desc: Use small objects in two colors, like red and white beans. Build one two-digit number in tens and ones, then build a second number the same way. Push them together and count the total. If you end up with 10 or more loose ones, group them into a new ten. Objects moving on the table make the new ten easy to see.

acts.name: Sidewalk Equations
acts.desc: Outside with chalk, write a two-digit problem in large columns on the pavement. Work through it together, writing the regrouped digit in a different color. The big size slows every step down and keeps each place visible. If you don't have outdoor space, use large paper on the floor.

acts.name: Build, Break, Rebuild
acts.desc: Build 28 with Snap Cubes: two trains of ten and 8 loose cubes. Ask your child to take away 9. There are only 8 loose cubes, so they break one train into ones, which makes 18 loose cubes. Now they take 9 away and read what's left: 19. Say, "We traded a ten for ten ones." Breaking the train makes subtraction regrouping visible.

focused.name: Tens and Ones Trading
focused.desc: Build a two-digit number with rods and units. Place a second number beside it. Count the units, and if there are 10 or more, trade ten of them for a new rod. Then count the rods for the tens. Go slowly and let your child lead the trade. Use this early in the concept when the hands-on trading is still doing the heavy lifting.

focused.name: Disc Regrouping
focused.desc: Build 47 with discs: 4 tens discs and 7 ones discs. Add 35 by setting down 3 more tens and 5 more ones. Ask, "Do we have enough ones to trade?" Your child swaps ten ones discs for one tens disc, then reads the total. A tens disc doesn't look like ten ones, so the trade has to happen in your child's head. This is the mastery activity: trading with discs instead of blocks means regrouping is understood, not just seen.

clicking.signs: Your child adds 38 + 25 and says "13 ones is 1 ten and 3 more" without being asked. They can show the trade with blocks or beans.
clicking.mixup: 38 + 25 = 513. They add 3 and 2, then 8 and 5, and write both answers side by side. Each column worked on its own, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build both numbers with blocks. Push the ones together and count 13. Ask, "Can 13 fit in the ones place?" Trade ten ones for a rod, then count all the rods.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on making 10 (Grade 1, Concept 6) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Multiplication with Equal Groups and Arrays
concepts.short: Multiplication with Equal Groups and Arrays
opening: Multiplication is not a set of facts to memorize. It is a way of counting smarter. When your child sees that 3 groups of 4 is the same as counting 4, 4, 4, they have the idea.
In 2nd grade, keep totals at 25 or under and use real objects every time.
concepts.before: Your child should skip count by 2s and 5s and know what it means to share objects into equal groups. If either feels uncertain, spend a few days on Concept 1 first. Equal groups are just skip counting you can hold.
concepts.quickwin: Put 12 crackers on the table. Ask your child to arrange them into equal groups, any way they like. Count the groups, count each group, and say it together: "3 groups of 4 is 12."
concepts.next: When your child can build an array and find the total without counting one by one, they are ready for Concept 5: How to Teach Your Child Division with Fair Sharing and Equal Groups. Division is multiplication looked at from the other side.

acts.name: Equal Group Parade
acts.desc: Call out a grouping, like "3 groups of 2." Your child claps twice, pauses, claps twice, pauses, claps twice. Count all the claps together. Switch to stomps or jumps and change the grouping each round. The pause between groups is what makes them equal groups.

acts.name: Equal Groups Chant
acts.desc: Pick one group size for the day and chant it with a clap: "One group of 2 is 2. Two groups of 2 is 4." Keep going up to 5 groups. Let your child pick tomorrow's group size. One size a day, repeated all week, sticks better than many at once.

acts.name: Array Art
acts.desc: Your child draws arrays on paper with dots or stamps, one array per box. Underneath each one they write the story: "2 rows of 5 is 10." Hang them up. When a matching fact comes up in conversation, point to the drawing.

acts.name: Equal Groups Story Time
acts.desc: Take turns making up equal group stories. "There are 4 frogs and each one has 2 flies. How many flies altogether?" Your child acts it out with whatever is nearby and tells you the answer. Let them make up stories too. Their versions are usually sillier, and they remember them longer.

acts.name: Snack Arrays
acts.desc: Serving crackers or grapes? Arrange them in rows before eating. "We have 3 rows of 5. How many is that?" Let your child arrange the next snack and tell you the story.

acts.name: Array Walk
acts.desc: Arrays are everywhere outside, like windows on a building or eggs in a carton at the store. Point one out and ask your child to find the total without counting one by one. "4 rows of 5 windows. How many windows?" Soon your child will start spotting arrays on their own.

acts.name: Build an Array
acts.desc: Give your child a pile of buttons or dried pasta. Call out, "Build me 4 rows of 3." They arrange neat rows and count the total. Then ask, "Can you turn it into a different array with the same total?" Turning 4 rows of 3 into 3 rows of 4 is a big idea worth sitting with.

focused.name: Array Building
focused.desc: Call out a situation, like 3 rows of 4, and have your child build it as an array, snapping each row into a train. Count by rows first, then count all. Turn the whole array a quarter turn and ask, "Is it still the same amount? What changed?" The turn shows that 3 rows of 4 and 4 rows of 3 match, without a rule to remember. Use this early in the concept when the physical building is still doing the heavy lifting.

focused.name: Every Way to Group
focused.tool: Three Bear Family Counters by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Count out 12 bears. Ask your child to find every way to split them into equal groups. They might find 2 groups of 6, 3 groups of 4, 4 groups of 3 and 6 groups of 2. Say each story out loud before moving on, then try 16 or 20 bears. This is the mastery activity: finding several equal-group stories for one total means multiplication is flexible, not a fixed fact.

books.title: Too Many Kangaroo Things to Do!
books.author: Stuart J. Murphy

clicking.signs: Your child looks at 3 rows of 5 and counts "5, 10, 15" instead of counting every dot. They can tell you 3 groups of 5 and 5 groups of 3 make the same total.
clicking.mixup: "3 groups of 5 is 8." They see two numbers and add them, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build it. Put out 3 plates with 5 crackers on each. Ask, "How many crackers are on the table?" Count by 5s together and compare the answer to 8.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on skip counting by 2s and 5s (Grade 2, Concept 1) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Division with Fair Sharing and Equal Groups
concepts.short: Division with Fair Sharing and Equal Groups
opening: Division is what happens when your child asks, "How do we split this evenly?" They have been sharing snacks for years. This concept gives that instinct a name and a structure.
Keep totals at 25 or under and use real objects every time.
concepts.before: Your child should understand equal groups from Concept 4 and skip count by 2s and 5s. If equal groups still feel fuzzy, spend a few more days on Concept 4. Sharing only makes sense once your child can see equal groups.
concepts.quickwin: Put 12 small objects on the table. Ask your child to share them equally between two cups. Count each cup and say, "12 shared between 2 is 6 each."
concepts.next: When your child can share a total into equal groups and connect it to a multiplication fact they know, the number work is complete. Concept 6: How to Teach Your Child to Compose and Decompose Shapes starts something new: a break from numbers to build with shapes.

acts.name: Fair Share Hop
acts.desc: Set out 3 cushions as friends. Call out a number of hops, like 12. Your child hops onto each cushion in turn, around and around, while you count each landing out loud. When all 12 hops are used, ask, "How many hops did each cushion get?" Going around in turn is exactly how dealing works.

acts.name: Sharing Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant that links sharing to equal groups: "12 shared by 3 is 4 each, because 3 groups of 4 make 12." Clap a beat and let your child swap the numbers each round.

acts.name: Division Story Drawing
acts.desc: Your child draws a sharing story, like 15 fish shared among 3 bowls. They draw the bowls, deal the fish in one at a time and write the number in each bowl. Underneath they write the story: "15 shared among 3 is 5 each." Let them pick what to share. Their own stories stick longer than yours.

acts.name: The Sharing Shop
acts.desc: Set up a pretend shop where your child is the shopkeeper. Ask for equal bags: "I need 4 bags with the same number of beads, and I have 20 beads." They count and pack. Change the totals and the number of bags each round. Keep the numbers small so the sharing is the focus, not the counting.

acts.name: Snack Sharing
acts.desc: Before snack time, tell your child how many people are eating and let them share the food equally. If it doesn't divide evenly, talk about the leftovers: "We have 14 crackers for 3 people. What's left over?" Leftovers are a natural part of real sharing.

acts.name: Sidewalk Division
acts.desc: Draw 3 or 4 circles on the driveway and collect small stones. Call a total and have your child drop the stones into the circles one at a time, around and around. Count each circle when done. If there are leftovers, set them aside and talk about them. If you don't have outdoor space, use paper plates on the floor.

acts.name: Toy Deal
acts.desc: Gather small toys and set out 2 to 4 containers. Your child deals the toys one at a time into the containers until none are left. Count each one and ask, "Were they equal?" This is division by dealing, the same way cards are shared in a game.

focused.name: Bear Sharing
focused.tool: Three Bear Family Counters by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Count out a set of bears, like 15, and set out 3 cups. Your child deals the bears one at a time into the cups until none are left. Ask, "How many in each cup? How do you know they're equal?" Lining each cup's bears up in a row lets them check without recounting. Use this early in the concept when the physical dealing is still making division visible.

focused.name: Array Flip
focused.desc: Build an array together, like 4 rows of 5. Count the total. Now flip the question: "If I have 20 and I want 4 equal groups, how many in each group?" Your child answers with the same array. Using one model for both questions shows how multiplication and division connect. This is the mastery activity: moving between multiplication and division with the same array means your child sees them as two sides of one idea.

clicking.signs: Your child deals objects one at a time until they run out, then checks that every group matches. They can tell you 12 shared by 3 is 4 because 3 groups of 4 make 12.
clicking.mixup: Giving each friend 3 and keeping the rest. They pick a number that seems fair instead of dealing until the pile is gone, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Deal together, out loud: "One for you, one for you, one for you." Keep going until the pile is empty. Then line up each share side by side to check.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days building equal groups (Grade 2, Concept 4) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Compose and Decompose Shapes
opening: Composing and decomposing shapes is how your child learns that shapes can be built from smaller pieces and broken into parts. This thinking shows up later in area and fractions.
Right now it just needs to feel like building and taking apart.
concepts.before: Your child should name basic flat shapes like squares and triangles and spot them in different sizes and turns. If shape names feel uncertain, spend a few days spotting shapes around the house (Grade 1, Concept 7). Building with shapes is easier once your child can name the pieces.
concepts.quickwin: Fold a square of paper corner to corner and cut along the fold. Ask, "What two shapes did we make?" Then put them back together and ask what shape they make now.
concepts.next: When your child can build a shape from smaller pieces and split a shape into parts, they are ready for Concept 7: How to Teach Your Child to Tell Time to 5-Minute Intervals. Seeing a whole made of parts helps with the clock face, one circle split into 12 parts.

acts.name: Shape Stomp
acts.desc: Call out a shape. Your child walks it on the floor, making a sharp turn at each corner and counting the sides out loud: "Square: 1, turn, 2, turn, 3, turn, 4, turn." For a rectangle, two long sides and two short ones. Walking the shape makes sides and corners something they feel with their feet.

acts.name: Shape Collage
acts.desc: Cut simple shapes from paper in a few sizes. Your child arranges and glues them to make a picture, like a house from a square and a triangle. When finished, they point to each shape and name it. The picture is the geometry.

acts.name: Build a Shape
acts.desc: Use toothpicks for sides and small balls of playdough for corners. Your child builds a square or a hexagon on the table. Then ask, "Can you split it into two smaller shapes with one more toothpick?" And: "Can you join two shapes to make a new one?" The toothpicks make sides and corners physical and easy to change.

acts.name: Shape Detective
acts.desc: Your child searches the house for shapes hiding inside other shapes. A window might be one big rectangle made of four smaller ones. They sketch what they find in a small notebook. The detective role makes careful looking feel like a mission.

acts.name: Sandwich Geometry
acts.desc: Making a square sandwich? Let your child direct the cuts. Corner to corner makes two triangles. Cut one triangle in half again and you get two smaller triangles. Ask what shapes appear after each cut, and whether the pieces still make a square when pushed back together.

acts.name: Shadow Shape Hunt
acts.desc: On a sunny day, look at shadows outside. Ask your child to name a shadow's shape and find the object making it. "Can you find a smaller shape hiding inside that shadow?" If you don't have outdoor space, use a flashlight indoors in a dark room.

acts.name: Chalk Shape Building
acts.desc: Draw a large rectangle or hexagon on the driveway. Your child draws lines inside it to split it into smaller shapes, then names every shape they made. Try the reverse: draw small shapes side by side and have them trace one outline around the outside. If you don't have outdoor space, use large paper on the floor.

focused.name: Shape Puzzles
focused.tool: Wooden Tangram Puzzle by Melissa and Doug
focused.desc: Give your child the tangram pieces and a simple outline card. They fill the outline by fitting pieces together. Once solved, ask them to name every piece. Then remove one piece and ask what shape the gap makes. Use this early in the concept when the physical fitting is still making composition visible.

focused.name: Build and Break
focused.desc: Your child builds a large hexagon from smaller pattern blocks. Then ask, "Can you make the same hexagon with different pieces?" Six triangles fill it. So do two trapezoids. The colors make it easy to see which pieces are which. This is the mastery activity: rebuilding the same shape with different pieces means your child sees that a shape can be made more than one way.

books.title: Captain Invincible and the Space Shapes
books.author: Stuart J. Murphy

books.title: When a Line Bends... A Shape Begins
books.author: Rhonda Gowler Greene

clicking.signs: Your child fills a tangram outline and names each piece they used. They can show two different ways to build the same hexagon.
clicking.mixup: "That's not a square anymore," after a square is cut into two triangles and pushed back together. The cut line makes it look broken, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Trace the square on paper first. Cut it, then lay the two triangles back inside the traced outline. Ask, "Does it still fill the square?"
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days naming shapes by their sides and corners (Grade 1, Concept 7) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Tell Time to 5-Minute Intervals
opening: Telling time clicks when it has a reason to matter. Your child already lives by a schedule, from breakfast to bedtime.
Counting the minute hand by 5s connects the clock to moments they already know.
concepts.before: Your child should tell time to the hour and half hour (Grade 1, Concept 9) and skip count by 5s. If either feels shaky, spend a few days there first. Every 5-minute time is just skip counting around the clock.
concepts.quickwin: Point to a clock and ask your child what time it is. Then ask, "What time will it be in 15 minutes?" Count the minute marks together by 5s.
concepts.next: When your child can read a clock to the nearest 5 minutes and set the hands to a time you describe, they are ready for Concept 8: How to Teach Your Child About Money: Counting Coins and Making Change. Counting by 5s on the clock is exactly what counting nickels needs.

acts.name: Clock Walk
acts.desc: Tape a large clock face on the floor and write the numbers 1 to 12. Your child stands in the middle and walks the minute hand to the time you call: "Show me 3:25." They count by 5s as they pass each number. The full-body clock makes the circle of minutes concrete before any paper clock.

acts.name: Time Check Routine
acts.desc: Pick two moments in your day, like leaving the house and starting bedtime. Make it your child's job to check the clock and report the time. Real clocks at real moments build the habit fast.

acts.name: Schedule Artist
acts.desc: Your child draws their day as a row of clocks: waking up, lunch, a favorite activity and bed. They draw the hands and write the time under each one. Hang it up so they can check their drawings against the real clock.

acts.name: Time Keeper Game
acts.desc: Your child runs the schedule for a pretend day. Give them made-up events and times, and they set a clock to each one and announce it: "Rocket launch at 2:35. Everyone to your seats!" Swap roles so they get to invent the schedule too.

acts.name: Kitchen Clock Check
acts.desc: Before a kitchen job like washing dishes, ask your child to check the clock and say what time it will be in 10 minutes. When you finish, they check again. "Were you right?" Guessing and checking makes the clock feel useful.

acts.name: Outdoor Time Guess
acts.desc: Note the time together before going outside. While you are out, ask your child to guess how long you've been outside. Check the clock when you come back in and talk about how close the guess was. This builds a feel for how long minutes last.

acts.name: Minute Hand Counting
acts.desc: Set a clock you can move to a time on a 5-minute mark. Ask your child to count around from the 12 to the minute hand by 5s: "5, 10, 15, 20. The minute hand is on the 4, so it's 20 minutes past." Doing this slowly with a real clock beats drawing hands on paper.

focused.name: Clock Setting
focused.desc: Set a time and ask your child to read it. Then say a time in words, like "twenty minutes after four," and have them set the hands. Work both ways: clock to words and words to clock. Watch how the hour hand creeps forward as the minute hand goes around. Use this early in the concept when the moving hands are still showing how minutes and hours connect.

focused.name: Analog and Digital Match
focused.tool: Turn and Tell Wooden Clock by Melissa and Doug
focused.desc: Say a time and have your child set the hands without looking at the digital windows. When they're done, they check the windows to see if they matched. Then flip it: set a time yourself, cover the windows and have them read the hands. This is the mastery activity: setting any 5-minute time and checking it on their own means your child can read a clock, not just recite it.

books.title: Telling Time with Big Mama Cat
books.author: Dan Harper

clicking.signs: Your child reads 4:35 by counting the minute hand by 5s from the 12. They point to the 7 and say "35" without counting every mark.
clicking.mixup: Reading 4:35 as 4:07, because the minute hand points at the 7. The number on the clock face is right there, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Write the 5s around the outside of a paper clock: 5 next to the 1, 10 next to the 2, all the way to 55. Count together from the 12 to the minute hand. After a week, cover the outside numbers and see if your child still knows them.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on hours and half hours (Grade 1, Concept 9) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child About Money: Counting Coins and Making Change
opening: Money is one of the most motivating places to do math because it is real. Your child already knows coins matter.
This concept teaches them to count a mix of coins and figure out change, skills they will use for life.
concepts.before: Your child should skip count by 5s and 10s and know pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters by sight. If coin names or values are still fuzzy, spend a few days handling real coins and saying their values. Counting coins is skip counting with a different number on each coin.
concepts.quickwin: Empty a coin jar onto the table. Ask your child to find the dimes and count them by 10s. Then add the nickels by 5s. Just those two coins to start.
concepts.next: When your child can count a mix of coins and build an amount more than one way, they are ready for Concept 9: How to Teach Your Child to Measure in Inches, Feet, and Centimeters. Careful counting with coins carries straight over to reading a ruler.

acts.name: Coin Hop
acts.desc: Draw a penny, nickel, dime and quarter on separate sheets of paper and write the value under each. Lay them on the floor. Call out an amount, like 30 cents, and your child hops onto coins that make that total, saying the running total with each landing. Change the amount each round. Hopping slows the counting down so each coin gets attention.

acts.name: Coin Rubbings
acts.desc: Place coins under thin paper and rub a crayon over them. Label each rubbing with the coin's name and value. Your child arranges them from least to greatest value and hangs the chart on the wall.

acts.name: Piggy Bank Sort
acts.desc: Give your child a pile of mixed coins and four cups labeled 1¢, 5¢, 10¢ and 25¢. They sort the coins, count each cup, then add the cup totals. Sorting first lets them focus on one coin type at a time.

acts.name: Checkout Line
acts.desc: Set up a store with household items and price tags under $1. Give your child real coins. They count out the exact price, and you play cashier. Then swap so they make change for you.

acts.name: Snack Shop
acts.desc: Set up a snack shop at the kitchen table. A cracker costs 5 cents and a grape costs 10 cents. Give your child 50 cents to spend. They choose, pay and get change back. Keep prices simple so the coins are the challenge, not the adding.

acts.name: Sidewalk Coin Store
acts.desc: Gather pebbles and leaves and set up an outdoor store. Price each item at 5 or 10 cents. Your child pays with real coins. The outdoor store feels like a market, not a lesson. If you don't have outdoor space, set up the same store at the kitchen table.

acts.name: Price Tag Hunt
acts.desc: At the store, point to a price under $1 and ask your child which coins they would use. "This costs 45 cents. What coins make that?" There's more than one right answer, and finding different ones is worth celebrating.

focused.name: Coin Counting
focused.tool: Pretend and Play Money by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Sort a mixed pile of coins by type. Count the dimes by 10s, then keep going with the nickels by 5s. Add the pennies last. Then ask, "Can you make 37 cents without any dimes?" The rule is where the thinking happens. Use this early in the concept when sorting and counting are still being built.

focused.name: Coin Trading
focused.desc: Play Money Bags together. Each turn, players collect or pay out coins. Whenever you can, trade smaller coins for a bigger one of the same value, like five pennies for a nickel. Before each trade, ask your child to prove the two amounts match. This is the mastery activity: making the same amount with different coins and explaining why they match means your child understands coin value, not just coin names.

books.title: Alexander, Who Used to Be Rich Last Sunday
books.author: Judith Viorst

clicking.signs: Your child counts a quarter, a dime and two pennies as "25, 35, 36, 37" without help. They can make 30 cents two different ways.
clicking.mixup: "A nickel is worth more than a dime, because it's bigger." Bigger usually means more, so this mistake makes sense.
