clicking.todo: Line up 5 pennies next to a nickel and 10 pennies next to a dime. Ask, "Which row of pennies is longer?" A coin is worth the pennies it stands for, not its size.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days skip counting by 5s and 10s (Grade 2, Concept 1) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Measure in Inches, Feet, and Centimeters
concepts.short: Measure in Inches, Feet, and Centimeters
opening: Measurement makes sense the moment it connects to something real. Your child already knows some things are longer than others.
This concept gives them a ruler and the words to say exactly how much longer, the same way every time.
concepts.before: Your child should line up the ends of two objects before comparing them and measure with small objects like paper clips (Grade 1, Concept 8). If that feels new, spend a few days there first. A ruler is just a row of equal units lined up for you.
concepts.quickwin: Find a crayon and a pencil. Ask your child which is longer. Then measure both with a ruler and say the lengths out loud: "The pencil is 7 inches. The crayon is 4 inches. The pencil is 3 inches longer."
concepts.next: When your child can measure an object with a ruler and compare two lengths, they are ready for Concept 10: How to Teach Your Child to Create and Read Graphs. The careful counting and recording they practiced here is what graphing asks for.

acts.name: Body Measurement Walk
acts.desc: Measure with body parts first. Walk the length of a room in heel-to-toe steps, then measure the couch in hand spans. Measure the same things with a ruler and compare. "My foot is about 7 inches. The rug is 6 of my feet. About how many inches is that?" Moving while measuring makes length feel like distance, which it is.

acts.name: Measurement Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant about units: "Inches for my fingers, feet for the floor, centimeters for tiny things, a ruler tells me more." Clap a beat and let your child change the examples. Matching each unit to real things keeps the choice of unit from feeling random.

acts.name: Measurement Art
acts.desc: Give your child a ruler and ask them to draw a picture made only of straight lines. Every line gets labeled with its length in inches or centimeters. When it's done, ask which line is longest and which is shortest. Labeling each line builds the habit of measuring carefully.

acts.name: Inchworm Walk
acts.desc: Your child walks two fingers along the table like an inchworm, exactly 1 inch per step, checking each step against a ruler. Set a finish line 12 inches away and count the steps. Then cover the same distance in 1-centimeter steps. Comparing the two counts shows how much smaller a centimeter is.

acts.name: Measure the Snack
acts.desc: Before cutting fruit or a sandwich, ask your child to measure it. "How long is this banana?" Measure in inches one day and centimeters the next. After cutting, measure a piece and ask, "How much shorter is it now?"

acts.name: Nature Measure
acts.desc: Outside, collect sticks and leaves. Your child guesses each one's length first, then measures in inches and lines them up from shortest to longest. "Is this stick closer to 4 inches or 8 inches?" Guessing before measuring builds a feel for length. If you don't have outdoor space, use household objects on the kitchen table.

acts.name: Furniture Measuring Expedition
acts.desc: Pick a room and measure the big things, like table height and door width. For long things, slide the ruler along and count how many feet it takes. Your child measures and you write the numbers down. Then ask, "Which is wider, the window or the door? By how many inches?"

focused.name: Ruler Practice
focused.tool: Inch by Inch Ruler by Junior Learning
focused.desc: Measure objects around the table, like a book and a pencil. Each time, your child lines up the zero end carefully, reads the number at the other end, and says the length in a full sentence: "This book is 9 inches long." Then measure the same objects in centimeters and ask, "Is that more or fewer centimeters than inches?" The answer surprises most kids. Use this early in the concept when lining up the ruler is still being learned.

focused.name: Centimeter Check
focused.desc: The white rod is exactly 1 centimeter long. Have your child measure a crayon in white rods, then check with the centimeter side of the ruler. Next, use the orange rod, which is 10 centimeters, to measure longer things and count by 10s. This is the mastery activity: matching rods to ruler marks means your child knows what each mark on a ruler stands for.

clicking.signs: Your child lines up the end of the object with the 0 before reading the ruler. They say the unit every time: "6 inches," not just "6."
clicking.mixup: Starting at the 1 instead of the 0, and reading 7 inches for a 6-inch pencil. Counting usually starts at 1, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Have your child put a finger on the 0 before placing anything. Then lay small cubes along the ruler from 0 to 6 and count the spaces, not the lines.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days measuring with paper clips and lining up ends (Grade 1, Concept 8) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Create and Read Graphs
opening: Graphs turn numbers into pictures. When your child can look at a bar graph and answer questions about it, they are doing real data work.
This concept is about collecting information and using it to answer questions your child cares about.
concepts.before: Your child should sort objects into groups and compare how many are in each (Grade 1, Concept 10). If sorting or comparing feels shaky, spend a few days there first. A graph is just sorted groups lined up so they're easy to compare.
concepts.quickwin: Ask everyone at home, "Apples or bananas?" Tally the answers on paper. Count each tally and ask, "Which got more votes? How many more?"
concepts.next: This completes the Grade 2 math core. Your child is ready for Grade 3, where multiplication facts and fractions build on everything here.

acts.name: Tally Walk
acts.desc: Pick one thing to count before a walk, like car colors. Your child keeps tallies on a small piece of paper as you walk. At home, count the tallies and talk about what you found: "We saw more blue cars than red ones. How many more?" The walk collects the data and the counting happens at the end.

acts.name: Graph Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Count it up and stack it high. Tall bars mean more, short bars mean fewer." Clap a beat and let your child change the words. Saying what a graph is for helps them ask questions about it, not just draw it.

acts.name: Sticker Picture Graph
acts.desc: Pick a topic your child cares about, like the weather this week. They collect the data, then build a picture graph with one sticker per item in each row. Label each row. When finished, they write one sentence about what the graph shows. That sentence is the hardest part and the most important.

acts.name: Survey Collector
acts.desc: Your child is a researcher with a clipboard. They write a question, like "Dogs or cats?", and ask everyone at home, stuffed animals included. They tally the answers and report back: "Most of our house likes dogs." Saying the results out loud builds the language of data.

acts.name: Breakfast Graph
acts.desc: Once a week at breakfast, count something on the table, like how many of each fruit are in the bowl. Your child draws a simple bar graph from the counts. Label the bars together and ask one question the graph can answer.

acts.name: Nature Data Collection
acts.desc: Outside, collect 15 to 20 leaves or rocks and sort them into groups your child picks. Count each group and build a graph when you get back inside. Choosing the groups makes the graph feel like their discovery. If you don't have outdoor space, sort a jar of buttons instead.

acts.name: Toy Sort Graph
acts.desc: Pull out a bin of toys and sort them by one thing, like color. Count each group. Your child draws a bar graph with one square per toy and compares the bars: "How many more red blocks than blue?" Sorting and graphing in one session shows how one leads to the other.

focused.name: Cube Bar Graph
focused.desc: Collect simple data, like how many of each color cube are in a bag. Stack one cube per count into a tower for each color and line the towers up side by side. Ask comparison questions before moving to paper. Use this early in the concept when the data and the graph need to be the same object.

focused.name: Pocket Chart Graph
focused.tool: Hundred Pocket Chart by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Use the chart as a graph. Give each column a category, like the kinds of shoes by the door. Your child slides one card into that column for each item counted. The pockets keep columns straight, so comparing heights is fair. Read the graph together and have your child write two questions it can answer. This is the mastery activity: building a graph from their own data and writing questions it can answer means your child knows what graphs are for.

clicking.signs: Your child reads a bar graph and answers "How many more?" by comparing the bars. They label each bar without being reminded.
clicking.mixup: Pointing to the tallest bar for every question, even "Which has the fewest?" The tallest bar stands out, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Turn the graph into cube towers. Ask your child to point to the shortest tower first, then the tallest. Ask one question about each before going back to the paper graph.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on sorting and comparing groups (Grade 1, Concept 10) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Place Value to 1,000
opening: Place value is the idea that where a digit sits in a number decides what it is worth. The 4 in 400 is worth something very different from the 4 in 40. Once your child really understands this, reading and comparing three-digit numbers stops being guesswork.
This clicks through real objects and real numbers, not drills.
concepts.before: Your child should count to 100 and know that a two-digit number has tens and ones. If they can look at 47 and tell you there are 4 tens and 7 ones, they are ready. If not, spend a few days on place value to hundreds (Grade 2, Concept 2) first.
concepts.quickwin: Find a grocery receipt and ask your child to point to a number in the hundreds and read it out loud.
concepts.next: When your child can read any three-digit number and tell you what each digit is worth without hesitating, they are ready for Concept 2: How to Teach Your Child Multiplication Facts (0-12). Strong place value makes multiplication click faster because your child already knows how numbers group.

acts.name: Number March
acts.desc: Call out a three-digit number and give each place a move: stomp for hundreds, clap for tens, tap your knees for ones. Say 342 and your child stomps three times, claps four times and taps twice. Switch roles so your child calls the number and watches you. Getting the order wrong on purpose makes them correct you fast, which is the best kind of practice.

acts.name: Place Value Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Hundreds on the left, then the tens, then the ones, that's how a number's done." Clap a beat and say it a few times. Ask your child to add a second line. Kids remember what they helped invent.

acts.name: Playdough Place Value
acts.desc: Roll playdough into a flat slab and scratch three columns into it with a pencil: hundreds, tens and ones. Call out a number like 253 and have your child press small playdough balls into each column to match. Read the number together, then let your child call one for you. It's messier than writing, and it sticks better because of it.

acts.name: Place Value Store
acts.desc: Set up a pretend store with price tags in the hundreds written on index cards. Your child is the clerk and you are the customer. Ask, "What does that cost? Is it more or less than this one?" The pretend store makes reading three-digit numbers feel useful.

acts.name: Receipt Reading
acts.desc: Pull out a grocery receipt or store flyer. Ask your child to find a number in the hundreds, read it aloud and tell you which digit is in the tens place. Then ask what would happen to the number if that digit changed to a 9. Receipts are real and already in your house.

acts.name: Sidewalk Place Value
acts.desc: Draw three large boxes on the pavement with chalk and label them hundreds, tens and ones. Call out a three-digit number. Your child hops into each box in turn, landing with both feet and saying that digit out loud. Then write the full number in chalk next to the boxes. If you don't have outdoor space, use masking tape on the floor indoors.

acts.name: Number of the Day
acts.desc: Write a three-digit number on a sticky note each morning and put it on the fridge. Ask small questions about it during the day: "What digit is in the hundreds place? What is ten more?" By dinnertime your child knows that number from every direction.

focused.name: Place Value Building
focused.desc: Call out two three-digit numbers and ask your child to build both side by side. Ask which is larger and how they can tell just by looking. Then move a flat from one number to the other and ask what changed. The size of the blocks makes each place's value visible before any written comparison. Use this early in the concept when the hands-on building still matters most.

focused.name: Flip and Change
focused.tool: Student Place Value Flip Chart by edxeducation
focused.desc: Flip the chart to a three-digit number and have your child read it aloud. Then say "10 more" or "100 more," and your child flips only the digits that change. Ask them to explain why the others stayed put. Try 10 more than 395 to see what happens when a 9 rolls over. This is the mastery activity: knowing which digit changes, and why, without building anything means place value is understood, not just practiced.

books.title: Sir Cumference and All the King's Tens
books.author: Cindy Neuschwander

clicking.signs: Your child reads 608 as "six hundred eight" and tells you the 0 means no tens. They can say what 10 more than 395 is and explain why two digits changed.
clicking.mixup: "10 more than 395 is 3,105." They add 10 to the 95 and write the result after the 3, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build 395 with blocks. Add one rod and count the rods: there are 10 now. Trade them for a flat. Ask, "How many flats now? How many rods?" Then write the new number: 405.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on place value to hundreds (Grade 2, Concept 2) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Multiplication Facts (0-12)
opening: Multiplication is a shortcut for adding equal groups. When your child multiplies 4 by 3, they are asking how much four groups of three add up to. That idea is the whole concept, and the facts are what happens when you know it well.
Most kids memorize tables before they understand what multiplication means. Start with the meaning, build it with objects and movement, and the facts follow with far less struggle.
concepts.before: Your child should add single-digit numbers confidently and skip count by 2s and 5s, then by 10s. If skip counting feels uncertain, spend time on it first (Grade 2, Concept 1). Skip counting is multiplication in disguise, and starting there makes everything easier.
concepts.quickwin: Put 3 small groups of 4 coins on the table and ask your child how many coins there are without counting one by one.
concepts.next: When your child can describe the equal groups behind a fact and recall the answer without counting up, they are ready for Concept 3: How to Teach Your Child Division Facts and Remainders. Division is multiplication in reverse, so every fact your child knows becomes a tool.

acts.name: Multiplication Jump
acts.desc: Pick a number and have your child jump while counting by it out loud. Jumping by 3s sounds like: jump, "3," jump, "6," jump, "9." Switch to stomping for 5s. Movement builds the skip counting that sits under every multiplication fact.

acts.name: Times Table Chant
acts.desc: Pick one fact family per day and make up a chant together. "Two, four, six, eight, who do we appreciate?" works for 2s. Let your child write the words for 3s and 4s. One family a day, repeated all week, builds faster than running through all twelve at once.

acts.name: Egg Carton Multiplication
acts.desc: Pull out an empty egg carton and a bag of dried beans. Call out a problem like 3 times 4. Your child fills 3 cups with 4 beans each and counts the total. The carton does the grouping, so equal groups are impossible to miss.

acts.name: Array Stamps
acts.desc: Cut a small square sponge into a stamp and press it into paint. Ask your child to stamp an array for a fact, like 3 rows of 4. Count the stamps and write the fact next to it. Then turn the paper sideways and ask what fact they see now. Seeing 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 in one picture shows that order doesn't change the answer.

acts.name: Multiplication Story
acts.desc: Make up a story together where the answer needs multiplication. "There are 5 dogs at the park and each one has 4 legs. How many legs is that?" Let your child add the next detail while you write the matching number sentence on a sticky note. The story shows the groups before any symbols get in the way.

acts.name: Sidewalk Array
acts.desc: With chalk outside, build an array on the pavement using rocks as markers. Call out a fact and have your child build it, then write the number sentence underneath. Ask them to draw a line through the middle and name the two smaller facts inside. If you don't have outdoor space, use stickers on a large sheet of paper on the floor.

acts.name: Multiplication War
acts.desc: Take a deck of cards and remove the face cards. Each player flips two cards and multiplies them. The higher product wins both pairs. When you disagree about which product is larger, work it out together before moving on. The game means many problems solved without it feeling like practice.

focused.name: Array Building
focused.desc: Call out a fact and have your child build the array with tiles. They write the fact, then turn the array and write the matching fact. Next, build a second array in a new color and push the two together to show how two small facts make a bigger one, like 3 × 4 and 3 × 2 making 3 × 6. Use this early in the concept when the visual grouping is still doing the heavy lifting.

focused.name: Fact Heroes
focused.tool: Times Tables Heroes by Orchard Toys
focused.desc: Play a round together. Each time a fact comes up, your child describes the groups before answering: "6 times 4 is 6 groups of 4." If they're stuck, they build it from a fact they know, like 5 groups of 4 plus one more group. This is the mastery activity: answering from memory and explaining the groups behind each fact means the facts rest on meaning, not just recall.

books.title: Too Many Kangaroo Things to Do!
books.author: Stuart J. Murphy

books.title: The Hershey's Milk Chocolate Multiplication Book
books.author: Jerry Pallotta

clicking.signs: Your child answers 6 × 4 and can tell you it means 6 groups of 4. When they forget a fact, they build it from one they know, like 5 × 4 plus 4.
clicking.mixup: "6 × 4 = 10." They see two numbers and add them, an old habit, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build it. Put out 6 cups and drop 4 beans in each. Ask, "Is it 6 plus 4, or 6 groups of 4?" Count by 4s together and compare.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on equal groups and arrays (Grade 2, Concept 4) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Division Facts and Remainders
opening: Division is the flip side of multiplication. When your child divides 12 by 3, they are asking how many groups of 3 fit inside 12. Every multiplication fact your child knows is a division fact waiting to be flipped.
Remainders are what is left when things don't divide evenly. They are not mistakes. They are part of the answer.
concepts.before: Your child should recall most multiplication facts and understand equal groups. If multiplication still feels uncertain, spend more time on Concept 2 first. Division built on shaky multiplication facts is harder than it needs to be.
concepts.quickwin: Put 15 crackers on the table and ask your child to split them equally among 3 people. Ask how many each person gets and how they figured it out.
concepts.next: When your child can divide any basic fact and explain what the remainder means, they are ready for Concept 4: How to Teach Your Child Multi-Digit Addition and Subtraction with Regrouping. The place value work from Concept 1 comes back as the engine for what's next.

acts.name: Division Freeze Dance
acts.desc: Call out a division problem, like "24 divided by 6!" Your child dances until they know the answer, then freezes and says it. If they're right, they pick the next dance move. Moving gives the brain a moment to find the fact without the pressure of sitting still.

acts.name: Division Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant that flips a multiplication fact: "3 times 4 is 12, so 12 divided by 3 is 4." Clap a beat and let your child swap the numbers each round. Practicing the two together builds the connection faster than practicing them separately.

acts.name: Remainder Art
acts.desc: Give your child 13 small objects and ask them to make groups of 4. They make 3 groups with 1 left over, then draw the groups on paper and circle the leftover. Ask, "What do we do with this one?" If 13 kids sit 4 to a table, one kid needs another table. The drawing makes remainders feel logical, not like an error.

acts.name: Division Story
acts.desc: Make up a story where the answer needs division. "We baked 18 cookies and need bags of 3. How many bags?" Let your child add the next detail and write the matching number sentence on a sticky note. When a remainder shows up, talk about what to do with it before writing anything down.

acts.name: Kitchen Division
acts.desc: Use real food to build division problems, like 12 grapes in 4 equal groups or 8 crackers shared among 3 people. The remainder is the snack nobody gets, which makes it memorable. Keep the numbers small enough to count every piece.

acts.name: Sidewalk Division
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw 3 or 4 circles on the pavement. Call out a total and have your child draw dots into the circles one at a time, around and around, until the total is used. Count each circle and the leftovers, then write the full division sentence underneath. If you don't have outdoor space, use paper plates on the floor.

acts.name: Division War
acts.desc: Take a deck of cards and remove the face cards. Each player flips two cards, uses the larger as the total and divides by the smaller. The bigger answer wins the round, and any remainder is simply said out loud: "9 divided by 2 is 4, remainder 1." The game packs many problems into a few minutes.

focused.name: Division Building
focused.desc: Give your child a number of cubes and ask them to split them into equal towers. Ask, "How many towers? How many in each? Any left over?" Then build the same total into a different number of towers and compare. Use this early in the concept when the physical grouping is still making division visible.

focused.name: Remainder Rectangles
focused.desc: Hand your child 17 tiles and ask them to predict how many full rows of 3 they can build and how many tiles will be left. Then build it and check: 5 rows of 3, with 2 left over. Try 17 in rows of 4, then rows of 5. This is the mastery activity: predicting the remainder before building means your child knows division facts well enough to see what's left without counting.

clicking.signs: Your child solves 20 ÷ 4 by thinking "4 times what is 20?" They can tell you what a leftover means in a real story, like one cookie nobody gets.
clicking.mixup: "17 ÷ 3 = 5," with the 2 leftovers forgotten. The answer looks finished once the groups are made, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Deal 17 beans into 3 cups. Before writing anything, ask, "Is anything still on the table?" Write the leftovers as part of the answer: 5, remainder 2.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on fair sharing (Grade 2, Concept 5) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Multi-Digit Addition and Subtraction with Regrouping
opening: Regrouping is what happens when a column adds up to more than 9, or when a column doesn't have enough to subtract from. A ten becomes ten ones, and a hundred becomes ten tens. The value stays exactly the same.
Most kids learn regrouping as a trick with arrows and crossed-out numbers. That trick works until it doesn't. Understanding why the digits change is what makes regrouping stick.
concepts.before: Your child should add and subtract two-digit numbers and understand place value to 1,000 from Concept 1. If two-digit regrouping still feels shaky, spend time on Grade 2, Concept 3 first. Regrouping without place value is just a procedure waiting to fall apart.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child to add 47 and 35 on paper and watch what they do when the ones add up to more than 9. That moment tells you exactly where to start.
concepts.next: When your child can trade in both addition and subtraction and explain what is happening to the digits, they are ready for Concept 5: How to Teach Your Child Fractions as Numbers.

acts.name: Regroup Stomp
acts.desc: Call out an addition problem where the ones add up to more than 9. Your child solves it column by column, right to left, and stomps once every time they trade ten ones for a ten. Switch to subtraction and stomp each time a column needs to trade a ten for ten ones. The stomp makes the trade a deliberate step instead of something rushed past.

acts.name: Regrouping Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Add the ones, if it's ten or more, trade it for a ten, that's what it's for." Clap a beat and say it before each session. Let your child add a line for subtraction.

acts.name: Base Ten Trade
acts.desc: Build a three-digit number with base ten blocks. Add another number by placing its blocks next to the first. When the ones pile reaches ten, swap them for a rod and move it to the tens. Your child can see exactly why the tens digit changes.

acts.name: Grocery Store Addition
acts.desc: Pick two items from a store flyer and ask your child to add the prices on paper, trading where needed. Then ask, "Can we buy both with $10?" Keep the numbers small enough that the focus stays on the trade.

acts.name: Change Back
acts.desc: Pretend to buy something for $1.47 and pay with $2.00. Your child works out the change on paper as 200 cents minus 147 cents, trading where needed. Then they check by counting back real coins. The coins make the subtraction easy to check.

acts.name: Sidewalk Equations
acts.desc: With chalk outside, write a three-digit problem on the pavement in large columns. Work through it together, writing each traded digit above its column in a different color. The large size slows each step down. If you don't have outdoor space, use large paper on the floor.

acts.name: Number Hunt
acts.desc: Open a store flyer and ask your child to find two numbers they think will need a trade when added. Write the problem and solve it. Then find two numbers that won't need a trade. Comparing the two kinds builds the habit of spotting a trade before it happens.

focused.name: Regroup and Build
focused.desc: Write a three-digit addition problem. Your child builds both numbers with blocks, then combines them column by column, trading ten units for a rod and ten rods for a flat when needed. Use this early in the concept when the hands-on support matters most.

focused.name: Across the Zero
focused.desc: Build 302 with discs: 3 hundreds, no tens and 2 ones. Ask your child to take away 147. There are no tens to trade from, so they first trade a hundred for ten tens, then a ten for ten ones. Have them say each trade out loud before moving a disc. This is the mastery activity: subtracting across a zero means your child understands the trades, not just the steps on paper.

clicking.signs: Your child solves 302 − 147 and can explain each trade in words. They spot which problems will need a trade before starting.
clicking.mixup: "52 − 17 = 45." In the ones column they take 2 from 7, the smaller digit from the bigger one, whichever is on top. That rule worked before, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build 52 with blocks and try to take away 7 ones. Ask, "Do we have 7 ones?" Trade a rod for ten ones, then take 7 away. Write the trade on paper only after the blocks show it.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on two-digit regrouping (Grade 2, Concept 3) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Fractions as Numbers
opening: A fraction is a number, not just a piece of a picture. When your child sees 1/2, they are looking at a point on the number line, more than 0 and less than 1. The bottom number tells how many equal parts the whole is split into, and the top number tells how many of those parts you have.
Most fraction confusion starts with pictures. Seeing that 2/4 and 1/2 land on the same spot is what turns fractions into real numbers.
concepts.before: Your child should understand equal parts and recognize halves and fourths by sight. If splitting shapes into equal pieces feels uncertain, spend time cutting real objects first (Grade 2, Concept 6). A piece that is almost half is not half, and that precision matters.
concepts.quickwin: Fold a piece of paper in half, then in half again. Open it and ask your child how many equal parts they see and what each part is called.
concepts.next: When your child can place a fraction on a number line and explain what the top and bottom numbers mean, they are ready for Concept 6: How to Teach Your Child Perimeter. Measuring around a shape uses the same careful attention to equal units.

acts.name: Fraction Jump
acts.desc: Tape a number line on the floor from 0 to 1 and mark the middle as 1/2. Call out a fraction and have your child jump to where they think it lives. Then call out two fractions and ask which is closer to 1. The floor line makes fractions feel like places, not slices of pie.

acts.name: Fraction Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "The bottom tells the parts, the top tells how many." Clap a beat and run through it before any fraction activity. Let your child add a line. The words numerator and denominator stick faster inside a rhythm they helped write.

acts.name: Playdough Fractions
acts.desc: Roll two playdough bars the same length. Your child cuts one into halves and the other into fourths with a plastic knife, then names each piece. Line them up and ask, "Which piece is bigger, 1/2 or 1/4?" The answer is visible before any comparison on paper.

acts.name: Fraction Story
acts.desc: Make up a story where fractions appear naturally. "We made 8 muffins and ate 1/4 of them. How many did we eat?" Let your child act it out with real objects before writing anything.

acts.name: Kitchen Fractions
acts.desc: Measuring cups are the best fraction tool in the house. Pour 1/2 cup of water and ask whether 1/4 cup is more or less. Then ask, "How many quarter cups fit in a half cup?" and pour to check.

acts.name: Sidewalk Fraction Number Line
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw a long number line from 0 to 1. Your child marks and labels halves, then fourths. Ask which fractions land on the same spot. When 2/4 and 1/2 meet in the middle, that moment of discovery beats any explanation. If you don't have outdoor space, use a strip of masking tape on the floor.

acts.name: Fraction Compare
acts.desc: Write fractions on index cards and lay them face down in two piles. Each player flips one card from each pile and decides which fraction is larger. When you disagree, fold paper strips to check. The game builds a feel for comparing fractions.

focused.name: Fraction Building
focused.desc: Lay out the tiles and ask your child to find every set of pieces that equals one half. Then ask, "Which is larger, 1/3 or 1/4?" Build both and look. The tiles make equal fractions and comparisons visible without any drawing. Use this early in the concept when the hands-on support is still doing the heavy lifting.

focused.name: Pizza Fractions
focused.tool: Pizza Fraction Fun Game by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Play a round together. Before placing each slice, your child names another way to make the same amount, like two 1/8 slices for one 1/4. They check by laying the slices on top of each other. This is the mastery activity: naming equal fractions quickly in the middle of a game means fraction relationships are becoming automatic.

books.title: The Hershey's Milk Chocolate Fractions Book
books.author: Jerry Pallotta

books.title: Full House: An Invitation to Fractions
books.author: Dayle Ann Dodds

clicking.signs: Your child places 3/4 between 1/2 and 1 on a number line. They can tell you 1/3 is bigger than 1/4 because thirds are bigger pieces.
clicking.mixup: "1/8 is bigger than 1/4, because 8 is bigger than 4." With whole numbers, a bigger number means more, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Cut two paper strips the same length. Fold one into 4 equal parts and the other into 8. Hold one part of each side by side and ask, "Which piece would you rather have if it were cake?"
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days splitting shapes into equal parts (Grade 2, Concept 6) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Perimeter
opening: Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a shape. To find it, you add up the length of every side. The skill is not the formula but the habit of measuring carefully and not skipping a side.
Perimeter is everywhere once your child starts looking, like the edge of a rug or the frame of a picture.
concepts.before: Your child should add multi-digit numbers and measure with a ruler in inches and centimeters. If measuring with a ruler feels uncertain, spend time on Grade 2, Concept 9 first. Perimeter is only as accurate as the measuring underneath it.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child to measure one side of a book with a ruler and guess the other sides. Then measure all four and add them up.
concepts.next: When your child can find the perimeter of any shape by measuring and adding every side, they are ready for Concept 7: How to Teach Your Child Area. Perimeter measures the border and area measures what's inside.

acts.name: Perimeter Walk
acts.desc: Walk the edge of a room together, counting heel-to-toe steps as you go. Then walk the edge of a second room and ask which has the bigger perimeter. Walking makes perimeter a distance you feel before it becomes a sum.

acts.name: Perimeter Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Add up every side, go all the way around." Clap a beat before measuring anything that day. Let your child add a line. The chant builds the habit of going all the way around before stopping.

acts.name: Perimeter Art
acts.desc: Give your child graph paper and ask them to draw a few shapes along the grid lines. They count the squares along each side, write the length next to it and add all the sides. The grid makes measuring easy, so the focus stays on checking every side.

acts.name: Fence Builder
acts.desc: Use toothpicks as fence pieces and an index card as a pretend yard. Each toothpick is one unit. How many toothpicks go all the way around? Change the shape of the yard and count again. A fence with a missing side has a gap, so a skipped side is easy to spot.

acts.name: Room Designer
acts.desc: Your child is designing rooms for a new house, and every room must have a perimeter of exactly 24 units. On graph paper, they draw as many different rectangles as they can. Are any of them squares? The design challenge makes perimeter feel like a tool.

acts.name: Outdoor Perimeter
acts.desc: Go outside and measure the perimeter of something real, like a garden bed or a blanket on the grass. Use a tape measure and write down each side, then add them up. Before measuring a second object, ask your child to guess which perimeter is bigger. If you don't have outdoor space, measure a rug or a table indoors.

acts.name: Perimeter Compare
acts.desc: Cut a few index cards into different shapes and label each side with a length. Your child finds each perimeter and puts the shapes in order from smallest to largest. Sorting shows that perimeter is one number for the whole border.

focused.name: Perimeter Building
focused.desc: Stretch rubber bands across the pegs to make shapes. Count the spaces along each side and add them for the perimeter. Then ask your child to build two different shapes with the same perimeter. Use this early in the concept when the physical building supports the measuring habit.

focused.name: Tile Fences
focused.desc: Give your child 6 tiles. They push them together edge to edge and count the outside edges for the perimeter. Then ask, "Can you rearrange them to make the perimeter bigger? Smaller?" A straight line of 6 has a perimeter of 14, and 2 rows of 3 has 10. This is the mastery activity: changing the perimeter while the number of tiles stays the same means your child sees perimeter as the edge, not the inside.

books.title: Sir Cumference and the First Round Table
books.author: Cindy Neuschwander

clicking.signs: Your child touches each side as they add it, so none get skipped. They can find a missing side of a rectangle because opposite sides match.
clicking.mixup: Adding only the two labeled sides of a rectangle: 5 + 3 = 8. The other two sides have no numbers on them, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Have your child write a length on every side before adding anything. Then they trace around the shape with a finger, saying each number out loud: 5, 3, 5, 3.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days measuring with a ruler (Grade 2, Concept 9) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Area
opening: Area is the amount of space inside a flat shape. It is measured in squares because squares cover a flat surface with no gaps. To find the area of a rectangle, count the squares in one row and multiply by the number of rows.
Perimeter is the edge. Area is the inside. Building both with real objects before any formulas is the fastest way to keep them apart.
concepts.before: Your child should understand multiplication and find the perimeter of a simple shape. If multiplication facts still feel uncertain, spend more time on Concept 2 first. Area uses the same rows-and-columns thinking as an array.
concepts.quickwin: Lay 12 square sticky notes in a rectangle on the table and ask your child how many there are without counting one by one.
concepts.next: When your child can find the area of any rectangle and explain how it's different from perimeter, they are ready for Concept 8: How to Teach Your Child Elapsed Time.

acts.name: Area Stomp
acts.desc: Tape a rectangle on the floor and fill it with square pieces of paper. Your child stomps along one row counting squares, then counts the rows, and you multiply together. Then lift all the squares and ask, "What did we take away, the area or the perimeter?" The empty tape outline shows the difference.

acts.name: Area Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Squares in a row, times the rows, that's the area, now everyone knows." Clap a rhythm before any area activity. Let your child add a line about perimeter so the two sit side by side.

acts.name: Square Tile Art
acts.desc: Give your child square sticky notes or paper squares. Ask them to cover an index card or a placemat with no gaps and no overlaps. Count the squares and write the area. Then ask, "How many in one row? How many rows?" The counting and the multiplying should match every time.

acts.name: Room Carpet Designer
acts.desc: Your child is choosing carpet for a room and can only buy 24 squares. On graph paper, they draw every rectangle they can find with an area of 24. Which would make the best room and why?

acts.name: Sidewalk Area
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw a large rectangle and divide it into a grid of squares. Your child counts the squares in one row, counts the rows and multiplies. Then draw a second rectangle with the same area but a different shape and ask, "Do they look the same size?" If you don't have outdoor space, use graph paper on the floor.

acts.name: Area and Perimeter Sort
acts.desc: Write a few rectangles on index cards, each labeled with its side lengths. Your child finds both the area and the perimeter for each card. Then sort: which rectangles have the same area but different perimeters? Sorting keeps the two ideas separate.

acts.name: Outdoor Estimation
acts.desc: Find a flat surface outside, like a patio tile or a picnic blanket. Ask your child to guess how many sheets of paper would cover it, then test the guess. The gap between the guess and the count is where a sense of area grows. If you don't have outdoor space, use a rug or a table indoors.

focused.name: Area Building
focused.desc: Ask your child to build every rectangle they can with exactly 12 tiles. They sketch and label each one: 1 by 12, 2 by 6 and 3 by 4. Then ask which rectangle has the smallest perimeter. Use this early in the concept when hands-on building is still needed.

focused.name: Split the Shape
focused.desc: Make an L-shaped figure on the geoboard with a rubber band. Ask your child to find the area without counting every square. They stretch one more band to split the L into two rectangles, find each area by multiplying and add the two. This is the mastery activity: splitting a shape into rectangles and adding the areas means your child understands area as rows and columns, not just a formula.

books.title: Sir Cumference and the Isle of Immeter
books.author: Cindy Neuschwander

clicking.signs: Your child finds the area of a 4 by 6 rectangle by multiplying, not counting every square. They say "square units" and can tell you why area isn't the same as perimeter.
clicking.mixup: Adding the sides to find area, so a 4 by 6 rectangle gets an area of 20. Going all the way around is the last thing they learned, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build the rectangle with tiles. Count the tiles together: 24. Then trace the edge with a finger and count: 20. Ask, "Which number is the inside? Which is the edge?"
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on arrays (Grade 2, Concept 4) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Elapsed Time
opening: Elapsed time is how much time passes between a start and an end. It is not about reading a clock, which your child already knows how to do. It is about counting forward through time in chunks that make sense, the way you count forward on a number line.
The stumbling block is almost always the same: kids try to subtract times like regular numbers. Counting forward removes that confusion before it starts.
concepts.before: Your child should read a clock to the nearest five minutes and know the difference between a.m. and p.m. If telling time still feels uncertain, spend time on Grade 2, Concept 7 first. Elapsed time built on shaky clock reading turns into two problems instead of one.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child what time it is now and what time dinner will be. Ask how long until dinner, and talk through how they figured it out.
concepts.next: When your child can count forward from any start time to find how much time has passed and explain how they got there, they are ready for Concept 9: How to Teach Your Child to Measure and Estimate.

acts.name: Time Hop
acts.desc: Set a start time on a clock and call out chunks of time to move forward, like 30 minutes or 15 minutes. Your child hops once for each chunk and says the new time with each hop: "Start at 2:00. Hop 30 minutes, now it's 2:30. Hop 30 more, now it's 3:00." Hopping makes counting forward through time physical.

acts.name: Schedule Art
acts.desc: Give your child a long strip of paper and ask them to draw their day as a timeline, from waking up to bedtime, with a few events in between. Label each with a time. Then pick two events and work out how much time passes between them.

acts.name: Family Day Planner
acts.desc: Plan a real Saturday together. Look up when the library or the park opens and closes, and pick a few things to do. If swim class starts at 3:30 and you need to leave the park by 5:00, how much time do you have in between? Could you fit a 45-minute lunch? Real plans give real numbers.

acts.name: Baking Clock Watch
acts.desc: Next time you bake, ask your child to note the start time on the clock and predict when the food will be ready. Check together when it's done. With two things cooking at once, ask which finishes first.

acts.name: Walk Around the Block
acts.desc: Note the time when you leave for a walk around the block, and again when you get back. Your child works out how long the walk took by counting forward from the start time. Try a different route another day and compare. If you don't have outdoor space, track how long a load of laundry takes instead.

acts.name: Daily Schedule Sort
acts.desc: Write a few events from a school day on index cards with start and end times. Shuffle them. Your child puts them in order and works out how long each one lasts. Which is longest? The answers have to make sense within a real day, which builds good checking habits.

acts.name: Time Story Walk
acts.desc: Make up a story as you walk. "We left home at 3:45. It took 10 minutes to reach the corner. What time is it now?" Let your child add the next event and how long it takes. The story makes adding time feel natural.

focused.name: Time Jumps
focused.desc: Set the clock to a start time and ask your child to move the hands forward by an amount of time, saying each jump out loud. Then show a start and an end time and ask them to find the time in between by counting forward in chunks. Use this early in the concept when moving the hands still supports the counting.

focused.name: Number Line Time
focused.tool: Number Line Student Clock by hand2mind
focused.desc: Unroll the minute track into a straight number line. Give your child a start time and an end time, like 2:40 and 3:25. They mark the start, jump to the next o'clock (20 minutes), then start again from 0 on the track and jump to 25. Add the jumps: 45 minutes. Roll the track back into the clock to check. This is the mastery activity: counting forward across the hour on a number line means elapsed time is a skill, not a guess.

books.title: Telling Time with Big Mama Cat
books.author: Dan Harper

clicking.signs: Your child finds the time from 2:45 to 3:20 by counting forward: 15 minutes to 3:00, then 20 more. They check that the answer makes sense in a real day.
clicking.mixup: "3:20 − 2:45 is 75 minutes." They subtract like regular numbers, but an hour has 60 minutes, not 100, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Put the subtraction away. Draw a line with 2:45 at one end and 3:20 at the other. Jump to the next o'clock first, then to the end time, and add the jumps.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days reading clocks to 5 minutes (Grade 2, Concept 7) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Measure and Estimate
opening: Measuring is finding out how much there is using a standard unit. Estimating is making a smart guess first. A child who measures but never estimates can't tell when an answer is unreasonable.
In 3rd grade, schools measure weight in grams and kilograms and liquid in liters. At home you'll still use cups and pounds, so this concept uses both.
concepts.before: Your child should use a ruler and read the numbers on a simple scale. If lining a ruler up at zero still feels uncertain, spend a few days on Grade 2, Concept 9 first. The tool needs to feel easy before estimating can build on it.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child to guess the length of a spoon in inches, then measure it. Ask, "Were you close? What would you guess next time?"
concepts.next: When your child can guess a measurement closely and then measure to check, they are ready for Concept 10: How to Teach Your Child Patterns, Properties, and Simple Equations.

acts.name: Estimation Walk
acts.desc: Walk through one room and pick five objects. Before measuring, your child guesses each length in inches or centimeters, and you write the guesses down. Then measure each one and circle the guesses that were within one unit. Comparing the guess to the measurement is the whole lesson.

acts.name: Measurement Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together about units: "Grams for a grape, kilograms for me, liters for a bottle, cups for my tea." Clap a beat and let your child change the examples. Matching units to real things keeps the choice of unit from feeling random.

acts.name: Kitchen Measurement
acts.desc: Measure ingredients for a simple recipe together, using measuring cups and a kitchen scale. Ask your child to guess each amount before measuring: "About how many grams does this apple weigh?" Then check. The kitchen is full of measuring with no setup needed.

acts.name: Scavenger Measure
acts.desc: Write a few measuring challenges on slips of paper and hide them around the house: "Find something exactly 6 inches long." "Find something that weighs more than 1 kilogram." Your child finds an object, measures it and checks whether it matches. The hunt makes measuring feel like a puzzle.

acts.name: Bottle Liter Check
acts.desc: Find an empty 1-liter water bottle; the size is printed on the label. Ask your child to guess how many cups of water fill it, then pour to check. It takes a little more than 4 cups, so the cup they know helps them picture the liter school uses.

acts.name: Container Compare
acts.desc: Collect a few containers of different sizes, like a mug and a pot. Ask your child to put them in order from holds-the-least to holds-the-most before measuring. Then fill each with water using a measuring cup and count how many cups fit. Compare the order to the guess.

acts.name: Outdoor Estimation
acts.desc: Go outside and pick a few big things to measure, like the width of the driveway or the length of a car. Your child guesses in feet first, then measures with a tape measure. Bigger spaces build a feel for feet that a ruler on the table never quite reaches. If you don't have outdoor space, measure a hallway instead.

focused.name: Two Units, One Object
focused.tool: Inch by Inch Ruler by Junior Learning
focused.desc: Set out a few objects and have your child measure each one in both inches and centimeters, writing the two numbers side by side. Ask, "Which unit gives a bigger number for the same object? Why?" This shows that units are a choice, not part of the object. Use this early in the concept when the ruler itself is still being learned.

focused.name: Liter Estimation
focused.tool: Liquid Measurement Set by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Line up a few containers from the kitchen. Your child guesses whether each holds more or less than 1 liter, then uses the metric marks on the half-gallon jar to measure 1 liter and pours to check. Next, ask for a guess in cups and check with the cup measure. This is the mastery activity: choosing a sensible unit and guessing close before measuring means your child has a real feel for how much each unit holds.

clicking.signs: Your child guesses a book is about 10 inches long before measuring, and the guess is close. They choose grams for a grape and kilograms for a bag of flour without being told.
clicking.mixup: Saying a grape weighs about 5 kilograms. The word kilogram is new and the weight behind it isn't real to them yet, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Hand your child a 1-kilogram bag of flour or sugar to hold. Then hand them a grape. Ask, "Does this grape feel like the bag?" Let the bag become their picture of a kilogram.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days measuring length with a ruler (Grade 2, Concept 9) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Patterns, Properties, and Simple Equations
opening: A pattern is a rule that repeats, and an equation says two things are equal. Both ask the same question: what rule is at work here?
In 3rd grade, this means noticing that you can add numbers in any order and get the same answer, and that a box can hold the place of a missing number. This is the quiet beginning of algebra.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable with all four operations and know that equal means the same amount on both sides. If that still feels uncertain, spend time with a balance before moving on. The balance is the idea, not the symbol.
concepts.quickwin: Write 4 + 5 = __ + 4 on paper and ask your child to fill in the blank. Watch how they think about it.
concepts.next: This completes the Grade 3 math core. Your child is ready for Grade 4, where multi-digit multiplication and fraction work build on everything here.

acts.name: Pattern March
acts.desc: Clap a pattern and have your child continue it: clap, stomp, clap, stomp. Then make it harder: clap, clap, stomp. Switch and let your child make a pattern for you. Ask, "What is the rule?" Naming the rule out loud matters more than continuing the pattern.

acts.name: Properties Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Add in any order, multiply too, times one never changes you." Clap a beat before any equation activity. The ideas need to feel familiar before the vocabulary arrives.

acts.name: Balance Scale Art
acts.desc: Draw a large balance scale on paper. Write a number on one side and ask your child what could go on the other side to balance it. "If I put 12 on the left, what goes on the right?" Try 3 × 4 and 10 + 2. When both sides match, an equation is born.

acts.name: Pattern Rule Hunt
acts.desc: Write number patterns on index cards, like 5, 10, 15, 20 and 100, 90, 80, 70. Ask your child to find the rule and write the next two numbers. Then they make up a pattern for you to solve.

acts.name: Missing Number Kitchen
acts.desc: While setting the table, build equations from what's happening. "We need 12 forks and I've put out 7. How many more? Write it with a box for the missing number: 7 + □ = 12." The real situation makes the missing number worth finding.

acts.name: Outdoor Pattern Walk
acts.desc: Walk outside and look for patterns, like fence slats or windows on a building. Name the rule for each one and ask, "What would come next?" Look for a pattern that breaks and talk about why. If you don't have outdoor space, look for patterns in tiles or fabric at home.

acts.name: Equation Balance Game
acts.desc: Write an equation on a strip of paper and fold it to hide one side. Show the visible side and ask your child what the hidden side must be to balance it. Try equations with multiplication and division too. Put the missing number on the left sometimes, which changes the thinking.

focused.name: Balancing Act
focused.desc: Hang a weight on the 9 peg and another on the 3 peg on one side. Ask your child to balance it on the other side. They might use one weight on 12, or weights on 10 and 2. Write each way as an equation: 9 + 3 = 12 and 9 + 3 = 10 + 2. Use this early in the concept when feeling the balance still matters.

focused.name: Missing Number Cards
focused.desc: Remove the face cards. Choose three cards that work together, like 4, 5 and 9, and lay them out as 4 + □ = 9 with the 5 face down. Your child finds the hidden card and flips it to check. Then try multiplication, like 3 × □ = 12, and put the hidden card on either side. This is the mastery activity: finding a missing number from either side of the equal sign means your child sees equal as a balance, not a signal to write an answer.

clicking.signs: Your child fills in 4 + 5 = __ + 4 with 5 and can explain why. They name the rule in a pattern before giving the next number.
clicking.mixup: Writing 9 in 4 + 5 = __ + 4. They see the equal sign as "write the answer here," so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build both sides on the Number Balance or with two piles of beans. Ask, "Do both sides balance if the blank is 9?" Change the blank until they do.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days comparing and evening out two groups (Grade 1, Concept 2) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Place Value with Large Numbers (to 1,000,000)
opening: Place value is the same idea it was in earlier grades: where a digit sits decides what it is worth. What changes in 4th grade is the scale. Your child now works with numbers up to one million.
Once your child sees that every place is ten times the place to its right, large numbers stop being intimidating.
concepts.before: Your child should read and write any three-digit number and tell you what each digit is worth. If place value to 1,000 still feels uncertain, go back to Grade 3, Concept 1 and the base ten blocks before moving here. Rushing into larger numbers on a shaky foundation makes everything slower.
concepts.quickwin: Find a news article or store flyer with a number in the hundred-thousands. Ask your child to read it out loud and tell you which digit is in the ten-thousands place.
concepts.next: When your child can read any number up to one million and tell you what each digit is worth without hesitating, they are ready for Concept 2: How to Teach Your Child Factors, Multiples, and Prime Numbers.

acts.name: Number March
acts.desc: Call out a six-digit number and give each place a move: stomp for hundred-thousands, clap for ten-thousands, jump for thousands, tap shoulders for hundreds, snap for tens and tap knees for ones. Say 342,561 and your child stomps three times, claps four times and keeps going through all six moves. Switch roles so your child calls the number. Getting a place wrong on purpose makes them catch your mistake fast.

acts.name: Place Value Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, hundred-thousands, that is how a big number's done." Clap a beat and say it a few times, then try it backwards. Let your child change one line. The backwards version builds real flexibility.

acts.name: Playdough Place Value
acts.desc: Roll six small playdough balls and line them up. Put an index card in front of each one with its place name. Call out a six-digit number and have your child press the right number of marks into each ball with a toothpick. The careful pressing gives every digit attention before anything is written.

acts.name: Place Value Store
acts.desc: Set up a pretend store where things cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, like houses and boats. Your child is the banker. "I want to spend two hundred fifty thousand dollars. How would you write that?" Swap roles. Pretend money makes reading and writing large numbers feel useful.

acts.name: Newspaper Number Hunt
acts.desc: Pull out a newspaper or real estate flyer. Ask your child to find five numbers larger than 10,000 and read each one aloud. For each one, ask which digit is in the thousands place and which is in the ten-thousands place. Real numbers make the skill feel worth having.

acts.name: Sidewalk Place Value
acts.desc: Draw six large boxes in a row on the pavement and label them, from right to left, ones up to hundred-thousands. Call out a number and have your child hop through the boxes from left to right, saying each digit out loud. Then write the full number in chalk beside the boxes. If you don't have outdoor space, use strips of paper on the floor indoors.

acts.name: Number of the Day
acts.desc: Write a six-digit number on a sticky note and put it on the fridge each morning. Ask small questions during the day: "What digit is in the ten-thousands place? What is ten thousand more?" By dinnertime your child knows that number from every angle.

focused.name: Place Value Building
focused.desc: Base ten blocks stop at thousands, so start there. Call out two four-digit numbers and have your child build both side by side, trading ten smaller pieces for one larger piece when needed. Ask which number is larger and how they can tell by looking. Then ask, "What would ten of these big cubes make?" That question carries the pattern up to ten-thousands. Use this early in the concept when the hands-on building still matters most.

focused.name: Flip and Change
focused.tool: Student Place Value Flip Chart (Millions) by edxeducation
focused.desc: Flip the chart to a six-digit number and have your child read it aloud. Then say "10,000 more" or "100,000 more," and your child flips only the digits that change. Ask why the others stayed put. Try 10,000 more than 295,400 to see what happens when a 9 rolls over. This is the mastery activity: knowing which digits change, and why, means your child understands place value at any size.

books.title: Sir Cumference and All the King's Tens
books.author: Cindy Neuschwander

books.title: Can You Count to a Googol?
books.author: Robert E. Wells

clicking.signs: Your child reads 405,027 as "four hundred five thousand, twenty-seven" without stopping. They can tell you the 5 is worth 5,000.
clicking.mixup: Writing four hundred five thousand, twenty-seven as 40,527. The zero they can't hear gets dropped, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Draw six boxes and split them with a comma into two groups of three. Write 405 in the thousands group first, then fill the ones group: 0, 2, 7. Every box gets a digit, even a zero.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on place value to 1,000 (Grade 3, Concept 1) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Factors, Multiples, and Prime Numbers
opening: A factor divides evenly into a number, and a multiple is what you get when you multiply it. A prime number is special: its only factors are 1 and itself.
These ideas are all about how numbers break apart and combine. They come back in fraction work later this year.
concepts.before: Your child should know multiplication and division facts and understand equal groups. If fact recall still feels uncertain, spend more time on Grade 3, Concepts 2 and 3 first. Finding factors means running through division facts quickly, so the facts need to be solid.
concepts.quickwin: Put 12 small objects on the table and ask your child to arrange them into equal rows in as many ways as they can. Each arrangement shows a factor pair.
concepts.next: When your child can list all the factors of a two-digit number and tell whether it is prime, they are ready for Concept 3: How to Teach Your Child Multi-Digit Multiplication.

acts.name: Factor Jump
acts.desc: Call out a number and have your child jump once for each of its factors, saying each one out loud. For 12: "1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12." Then switch to multiples: "Give me the first six multiples of 4," with a jump for each. Get a factor wrong on purpose and let them correct you.

acts.name: Multiple Chant
acts.desc: Pick one number per day and make up a chant for its multiples: "Four, eight, twelve, sixteen, twenty, that's the four-train running." Clap a beat before any activity that day. One number repeated all week builds more than all of them at once.

acts.name: Factor Rainbow Art
acts.desc: Your child writes the factors of 24 in order across a page: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Then they draw a colored arch joining each factor pair, starting with 1 and 24 on the outside and working in. Ask, "Is there ever a number that pairs with itself?" Try 36 to find out.

acts.name: Prime Detective
acts.desc: Your child is the prime detective. Call out a number and hand them that many coins. Their job is to arrange the coins into equal rows in any way other than one long row. "Can you arrange 7 into equal rows besides one row of 7? Then it is prime." The coins are the evidence.

acts.name: Kitchen Factors
acts.desc: When baking, turn the tray into a factor problem. "We have 24 cookies to arrange in equal rows. What are all the ways?" Work out the pairs together and pick the one that fits the tray best.

acts.name: Sidewalk Multiples
acts.desc: Draw a long number line on the pavement from 0 to 40. Circle the multiples of 4 in one color and the multiples of 6 in another. Where both colors land, you have common multiples. Ask, "What is the smallest number where both colors land?" If you don't have outdoor space, use masking tape on the floor with sticky notes.

acts.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
acts.desc: Write out a 10 by 10 grid numbered 1 to 100. Your child crosses out 1, circles 2 and crosses out every other multiple of 2. Then they circle 3 and cross out its multiples, and keep going. The numbers left standing are the primes. This one takes steady attention, so save it for when the earlier activities feel easy.

focused.name: Factor Building
focused.desc: Give your child a number of tiles and ask them to build every possible rectangle, with no gaps and no overlaps. Each rectangle shows a factor pair, so they sketch and label each one. Ask, "Which numbers can only be built as one long row?" Those are the primes, found by building rather than by definition. Use this early in the concept when the building is still making factors visible.

focused.name: Factor Moves
focused.tool: Prime Climb by Math for Love
focused.desc: Play a round together. Each time a piece lands, your child names the factors of that space before the next turn. The board colors every prime red, so ask them to predict whether a number is prime before checking its color. This is the mastery activity: naming factors and spotting primes in the middle of a game means the ideas are becoming automatic.

clicking.signs: Your child lists every factor of 24 in pairs without missing any. They can tell you 15 isn't prime because 3 rows of 5 works.
clicking.mixup: "9 is prime because it's odd." Many small odd numbers are prime, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Hand your child 9 coins and ask them to make equal rows other than one long row. When 3 rows of 3 appear, ask, "Is 9 still prime?"
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on division facts (Grade 3, Concept 3) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Multi-Digit Multiplication
opening: Multi-digit multiplication is still equal groups, just bigger. When your child multiplies 34 by 12, they are finding 12 groups of 34. The method is breaking the numbers apart by place value, multiplying the pieces and adding them back together.
Every written method is a shortcut for that idea. Understanding it is what separates a child who follows steps from one who knows what the steps mean.
concepts.before: Your child should know multiplication facts well and understand place value to at least four digits. If either feels uncertain, spend more time on Grade 3, Concept 2 or on Concept 1 here first. On shaky facts, multi-digit multiplication turns into memorized steps with nothing underneath.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child to multiply 23 by 4 by breaking it apart: "What is 20 times 4? What is 3 times 4? Now add them." That is the idea behind every method.
concepts.next: When your child can multiply two 2-digit numbers and explain what each partial product means, they are ready for Concept 4: How to Teach Your Child Multi-Digit Division. Division is multiplication in reverse, so every strategy built here carries over.

acts.name: Multiplication March
acts.desc: Write 23 × 4 on paper. Your child claps twice for the 2 tens and stomps three times for the 3 ones, then says what each part is worth: 20 and 3. Then solve together by multiplying each part by 4. Saying what each digit is worth before calculating gives the method its meaning.

acts.name: Break-Apart Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Break it by place, multiply each part, add them together, that's the whole art." Clap a beat before any multiplication session. Let your child rewrite the words.

acts.name: Array Art
acts.desc: Draw a large rectangle on graph paper for a problem like 24 × 13. Split it into four parts: 20 by 10, 20 by 3, 4 by 10 and 4 by 3. Your child colors each part and finds its area, then adds all four. The colored rectangle shows exactly where each partial product comes from.

acts.name: Store Multiplication
acts.desc: Set up a pretend store where things come in packs. "Juice boxes come in packs of 24. We need 13 packs for the party. How many juice boxes is that?" Work it out together and change the item through the week.

acts.name: Receipt Estimation
acts.desc: Pick one item from a grocery receipt. Ask your child to estimate the cost of buying it 15 times, then work out the exact answer and compare. Estimating first turns the exact answer into something to check.

acts.name: Sidewalk Multiplication
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw a large area model for a two-digit problem and label each section. Your child fills in each part and adds them up. The large size slows every step down. If you don't have outdoor space, tape a large sheet of paper to the floor.

acts.name: Multiplication Story
acts.desc: Make up multiplication stories as you walk or drive. "There are 18 apartments in that building and each has 14 windows. How many windows?" Your child calculates while you estimate, then compare. Switch roles for the next story.

focused.name: Area Model Building
focused.desc: Build a rectangle for 13 × 12: one flat, three rods along one side, two rods along the other and six units in the corner. The blocks fall into four sections by place value: 100, 30, 20 and 6. Your child counts each section and adds them to get 156. The blocks make every partial product visible before any written method. Use this early in the concept when the place value connection is still being built.

focused.name: Roll, Estimate, Multiply
focused.desc: Roll the number dice to get four digits and arrange them into two 2-digit numbers. Before multiplying, your child estimates by rounding each number to the nearest ten. Then they multiply with an area model and compare the answer to the estimate. This is the mastery activity: estimating first and checking after means multiplication is both accurate and sensible.

clicking.signs: Your child multiplies 24 × 13 and can point to where 20 × 10 shows up in their work. Their estimate and their answer land close together.
clicking.mixup: "24 × 13 = 212." They multiply 20 × 10 and 4 × 3, add them and forget the two middle pieces. Matching tens with tens and ones with ones works for adding, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Draw the rectangle and split it into four parts. Ask your child to find all four areas before adding anything. Count the parts together: there should always be four.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on area with rows and columns (Grade 3, Concept 7) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Multi-Digit Division
opening: Division still asks how many equal groups fit inside a total. In 4th grade, the numbers get bigger. Dividing 756 by 6 is the same question as 12 divided by 3, with more places to work through.
The key is sharing from the biggest place first, one place at a time, and trading when a place won't share evenly.
concepts.before: Your child should know division facts well and be comfortable with multi-digit multiplication from Concept 3. If either feels uncertain, spend more time there before moving here. Division leans on both at once, and a gap in either makes the work frustrating.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child to divide 84 by 4 in parts: "How many 4s are in 80? How many in 4? Add those answers." That breaking-apart idea is the heart of this concept.
concepts.next: When your child can divide a three-digit number by a one-digit number and explain what the remainder means, they are ready for Concept 5: How to Teach Your Child Equivalent Fractions.

acts.name: Division Freeze Dance
acts.desc: Call out a problem like "56 divided by 7!" Your child dances until they know the answer, then freezes and says it. If they're right, they pick the next move. Add bigger problems like 84 ÷ 4 as confidence builds.

acts.name: Sharing Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Share the hundreds, then the tens, then the ones, trade what's left, and then you're done." Clap a beat before every division session. Saying the order out loud keeps the place value thinking visible.

acts.name: Place Value Color Map
acts.desc: On a large sheet of paper, work through 756 ÷ 6 with each place in its own color: hundreds in red, tens in blue, ones in green. Your child writes how many of each place go into each group and what gets traded down. The colors show exactly where each part of the answer comes from.

acts.name: Packaging Story
acts.desc: Pretend you're packing orders. "We have 132 granola bars and boxes that hold 6. How many full boxes? Any left over?" Change the item each time, like crayons into sets. The leftovers always have a real meaning.

acts.name: Kitchen Division
acts.desc: Use a real recipe: "This makes 96 mini muffins and we want bags of 8 for a bake sale. How many bags?" Work it out on paper, then check with crackers as stand-ins.

acts.name: Sidewalk Division
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw 4 large circles and write 128 ÷ 4. Your child draws 1 hundred, 2 tens and 8 ones as simple symbols, then shares them into the circles, trading the hundred for ten tens when it won't share evenly. If you don't have outdoor space, use paper plates on the floor.

acts.name: Division Estimation Walk
acts.desc: Make up estimation problems from what you see. "That wall has about 200 bricks in rows of 8. About how many rows?" Estimate first, then work it out. Estimating first builds a sense of whether an answer is reasonable.

focused.name: Division Building
focused.desc: Give your child cubes for a problem like 52 ÷ 4. They snap the cubes into trains of 4 and count the trains. Any cubes left over are the remainder. Then work the same problem on paper and compare. Use this early in the concept when the physical grouping is still making division visible.

focused.name: Share by Place
focused.desc: Build 756 with discs: 7 hundreds, 5 tens and 6 ones. Draw 6 circles. Your child shares the hundreds first, one per circle, then trades the leftover hundred for ten tens and shares the tens. Keep going down to the ones. Count one circle to find the answer: 126. This is the mastery activity: sharing by place and trading when stuck means your child understands what every step of division is doing.

clicking.signs: Your child shares 756 by 6 starting with the hundreds and explains each trade. They check the answer by multiplying it back: 126 × 6 = 756.
clicking.mixup: "756 ÷ 6 = 12 with 36 left over." They stop after the tens and miss that the ones still need sharing, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Go back to the discs. Ask, "Is anything still outside the circles?" Keep sharing until every disc is used or only a few ones are left. Then multiply back to check.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on division facts and remainders (Grade 3, Concept 3) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Equivalent Fractions
opening: Equivalent fractions are different-looking fractions that name the same amount. One half and two fourths land on the same spot. Understanding this isn't a trick with multiplying the top and bottom. It's seeing that the same piece can be cut into more, smaller pieces.
That picture is what makes every fraction operation possible later.
concepts.before: Your child should know what the top and bottom numbers of a fraction mean and place fractions on a number line. If that still feels uncertain, spend time on Grade 3, Concept 5 first. Shaky fraction basics are the most common reason fraction work falls apart in upper grades.
concepts.quickwin: Fold a strip of paper in half, then in half again. Open it and ask how many equal parts there are. Then ask, "What do two of these parts equal?" They just found that 2/4 equals 1/2.
concepts.next: When your child can tell whether two fractions are equivalent and write a new equivalent fraction for any fraction, they are ready for Concept 6: How to Teach Your Child to Add and Subtract Fractions.

acts.name: Fraction Jump
acts.desc: Tape a number line on the floor from 0 to 1. Mark halves in one color and fourths in another, then add eighths. Call out a fraction and have your child jump to it. Then call out a different fraction for the same spot. When two jumps land together, your child shouts, "Equivalent!"

acts.name: Equivalent Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Cut every piece the same way, and the amount stays the same." Clap a beat before any fraction activity. Then ask what happens to the top and bottom numbers when every piece is cut in two.

acts.name: Fraction Strip Art
acts.desc: Give your child several paper strips of the same length. They fold and cut one into halves, one into fourths, one into eighths, one into thirds and one into sixths. Line them up under a whole strip and ask, "Which pieces are the same size?" Let them glue the strips into a chart and label each piece.

acts.name: Fraction Chef
acts.desc: Pretend you run a recipe kitchen. "The recipe calls for 3/4 cup, but our cup is marked in eighths. What do we measure instead?" Work it out with the fraction strips. Then try: "We only have a 1/3 cup and we need 2/6. Does it work?"

acts.name: Kitchen Fractions
acts.desc: Pour 1/2 cup of water into a clear glass. Ask your child how many 1/4 cups would fill the same amount, then pour to check. Measuring cups are the best equivalent fraction tool in the house.

acts.name: Sidewalk Fraction Number Line
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw a long number line from 0 to 2. Your child marks halves, thirds, fourths and sixths in different colors. Circle every spot where two fractions land together and ask, "What do you notice about these fractions?" If you don't have outdoor space, use masking tape on the floor with index card labels.

acts.name: Equivalent Fraction War
acts.desc: Write fractions on index cards and make two face-down piles. Each player flips one card from each pile and decides whether the two are equivalent. If they are, call it out and keep both cards. If not, the larger fraction wins. Check disagreements with the paper strips.

focused.name: Fraction Building
focused.desc: Ask your child to find every set of tiles that equals one half, then every set that equals three quarters. Fitting the tiles side by side makes equivalence something they discover, not calculate. Use this early in the concept when the hands-on matching is still building the picture.

focused.name: Domino Matches
focused.tool: Mastering Fractions Dominoes by Lakeshore Learning
focused.desc: Play a round together. Each time your child lays down a domino, they explain why the two ends match, like "2/4 is the same as 1/2 because each half is cut into 2." When unsure, they check with the fraction tiles. This is the mastery activity: matching equal fractions and explaining why means the idea is understood, not memorized.

books.title: Full House: An Invitation to Fractions
books.author: Dayle Ann Dodds

clicking.signs: Your child shows that 3/4 equals 6/8 with paper strips and explains why. They can write two more fractions equal to 1/2 without help.
