clicking.mixup: "2/3 equals 3/4, because you added 1 to the top and the bottom." Doing the same thing to both numbers feels fair, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Build both with fraction tiles and lay them side by side. Ask, "Are they the same length?" Then cut each third into two pieces and show that 2/3 becomes 4/6.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on fractions on the number line (Grade 3, Concept 5) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Add and Subtract Fractions
opening: Adding fractions works when the pieces are the same size. In 4th grade, the fractions share a bottom number, like 3/8 + 2/8. The bottom number names the size of the piece, so it stays the same. Only the count of pieces changes: 3 eighths plus 2 eighths is 5 eighths.
Mixed numbers, like 2 1/4, are whole numbers and fractions together. Adding them means wholes with wholes and pieces with pieces.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable with equivalent fractions from Concept 5 and know that the bottom number names the size of the piece. If that still needs support, spend more time on Concept 5 first. Fractions with different bottom numbers come in 5th grade, once this is solid.
concepts.quickwin: Cut a paper strip into 8 equal pieces. Hand your child 3 pieces, then 2 more. Ask, "How many eighths do you have now?" Write it together: 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8.
concepts.next: When your child can add and subtract fractions with the same bottom number, including mixed numbers, they are ready for Concept 7: How to Teach Your Child to Multiply Fractions by Whole Numbers. Fractions with different bottom numbers wait for 5th grade.

acts.name: Fraction Freeze Dance
acts.desc: Spread index cards with problems like 2/6 + 3/6 on the floor. Play music, and when it stops, call out one of the problems. Your child finds the card and works out the answer, taking as long as they need. If they're right, they pick the next dance move.

acts.name: Fraction Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Same-size pieces, add the tops. The bottom names the size, so the bottom stays put." Clap a rhythm before any fraction activity. Let your child add a line about subtracting.

acts.name: Paper Strip Fractions
acts.desc: Cut a few paper strips into eighths. Your child shows 3/8 + 4/8 by laying pieces end to end, then 7/8 − 2/8 by taking pieces away. Then try 5/8 + 6/8 and ask, "Is that more than one whole strip?" Laying 11 pieces against an 8-piece strip shows that 11/8 is 1 and 3/8.

acts.name: Fraction Kitchen
acts.desc: Run a pretend cooking show. "We need 1/4 cup of oats, then 2/4 cup more for the topping. How much altogether?" Your child works it out on paper, then measures with the 1/4 cup to check. Let them be the host who explains each step out loud.

acts.name: Measuring Cup Fractions
acts.desc: Pour 3/4 cup of water into a clear cup, then pour out 1/4 cup. Ask how much is left before checking. Then try mixed numbers: 1 1/4 cups plus 1 2/4 cups. Measuring makes each answer easy to check.

acts.name: Fraction Story Walk
acts.desc: Make up a running story as you walk. "We walked 2/4 of a mile, then 1/4 of a mile more. How far is that?" Add to the story at each corner while your child works out each answer out loud. With no cup to check against, this one is harder. If you don't have outdoor space, tell the story about laps around the kitchen table.

acts.name: Mixed Number Number Line
acts.desc: Draw a number line from 0 to 3 on a long strip of paper and mark every quarter. Ask your child to add 1 3/4 + 1/4 by jumping forward, then 2 1/4 − 3/4 by jumping back. Crossing a whole number on the line shows why 1 3/4 + 1/4 makes exactly 2.

focused.name: Tower Adding
focused.tool: Fraction Tower Cubes by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Snap together eighth cubes to show 3/8, then add 4/8 more. Your child counts the total and stands it next to a whole tower: 7/8 is one piece short. Then try a sum that goes past one whole and compare again. Use this early in the concept when the visual support is most helpful.

focused.name: Fill the Tubes
focused.tool: Fraction Formula Game by Educational Insights
focused.desc: Play using one size of piece at a time, like eighths only. Each time your child adds pieces, they say the new total out loud and how far they are from one whole: "5/8, so 3/8 to go." This is the mastery activity: tracking the total and the distance to one whole without the tower in front of them means fraction addition is understood.

books.title: Full House: An Invitation to Fractions
books.author: Dayle Ann Dodds

clicking.signs: Your child adds 3/8 + 2/8 and says "5 eighths" before writing anything. They can explain why the bottom number doesn't change.
clicking.mixup: "3/8 + 2/8 = 5/16." They add the tops and the bottoms the same way, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Lay out 3 eighth pieces and 2 more. Ask, "Did the pieces get smaller?" Count them together: 5 pieces, each still an eighth.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on what the bottom number means (Grade 3, Concept 5) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Multiply Fractions by Whole Numbers
opening: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number means taking that fraction several times. Three groups of 1/4 is 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4, which is 3/4.
The whole number tells how many times. The top number grows and the bottom number stays the same, because the size of the piece never changes.
concepts.before: Your child should add fractions with the same bottom number from Concept 6. If that still feels uncertain, spend more time there first. This concept is repeated fraction adding, so make that link out loud.
concepts.quickwin: Put 3 groups of 2 crackers on the table and ask how many crackers there are. Then measure 1/4 cup of water into 3 separate cups and ask how much water there is altogether.
concepts.next: When your child can multiply a fraction by a whole number and explain what the answer means in a real situation, they are ready for Concept 8: How to Teach Your Child About Angles and Geometric Figures.

acts.name: Fraction Number Line Hops
acts.desc: Tape a number line on the floor from 0 to 2 and mark the thirds. Call out "4 times 1/3." Your child starts at 0 and hops one third four times, calling out the total each time: "1/3, 2/3, 3/3, 4/3." Hopping makes repeated adding of fractions physical.

acts.name: Fraction Multiplication Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "The whole number counts the groups, the top number grows, the bottom stays." Clap a rhythm and let your child add a stomp between lines.

acts.name: Fraction Plate Art
acts.desc: Your child draws three circles the same size and shades 1/4 of each. Ask, "How much is shaded altogether?" They count the shaded parts across all three: 3/4. Then they write the number sentence under the circles: 3 × 1/4 = 3/4.

acts.name: Fraction Chef
acts.desc: Run a pretend restaurant. "One order of pancakes needs 2/3 cup of flour. We just got 4 orders. How much flour?" Work it out on paper, then measure with the 1/3 cup to check. Change the fraction and the number of orders through the week.

acts.name: Recipe Scaling
acts.desc: Find a simple recipe and ask your child to triple one ingredient. If it calls for 3/4 cup of sugar, how much is needed for three batches? They write the number sentence and solve it, then measure with the 1/4 cup to check.

acts.name: Sidewalk Fraction Hops
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw a number line from 0 to 4 and mark the fourths. Call out 5 × 3/4. Your child hops 3/4 at a time, five times, and circles where they land. Ask, "What does it mean that you landed past 3?" Landing past a whole number is the big idea here. If you don't have outdoor space, use a masking tape line on the floor.

acts.name: Fraction Multiplication Story
acts.desc: Make up stories together. "Each person at the party eats 2/3 of a pizza. There are 5 people. How much pizza?" Let your child make up the next one. Keep the fractions simple so the multiplying stays the focus.

focused.name: Tile Groups
focused.desc: For 3 × 1/4, your child lays three 1/4 tiles end to end under the whole tile. Ask, "How much of the whole do they cover?" Three of the four quarter spaces: 3/4. Then try 5 × 1/4 and see the tiles run past the whole. Use this early in the concept when the matching is still building understanding.

focused.name: Pizza Groups
focused.tool: Pizza Fraction Fun Game by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Play a round together. Before placing slices, your child says a multiplication sentence that matches them: "Two slices of 1/8 is 2 × 1/8, which is 2/8." This is the mastery activity: turning pieces into a multiplication sentence without prompting means the idea is understood, not just applied.

books.title: The Hershey's Milk Chocolate Fractions Book
books.author: Jerry Pallotta

clicking.signs: Your child solves 4 × 2/3 as 8/3 and can tell you that's 2 and 2/3. They show it on a number line with four hops.
clicking.mixup: "4 × 2/3 = 8/12." They multiply the bottom number too, the way both numbers get multiplied in a whole-number problem, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Lay out four groups of two 1/3 tiles. Ask, "Are these pieces thirds or twelfths?" Count the thirds together: 8 of them.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days adding fractions with the same bottom number (Grade 4, Concept 6) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child About Angles and Geometric Figures
opening: An angle is the amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point. A right angle is a quarter turn, or 90 degrees. Acute angles turn less and obtuse angles turn more.
Measuring with a protractor comes after your child understands what an angle is. Starting with the tool first is like learning a ruler before knowing what length is.
concepts.before: Your child should name basic shapes and spot a right angle by sight. If that still takes thinking, spend a few days pointing out square corners on books and doors first. The right angle is the reference point for everything here.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child to make a right angle with their arm and body. Then ask, "What would it look like if you opened your arm a little more? All the way?"
concepts.next: When your child can measure an angle with a protractor and draw one of a given size, they are ready for Concept 9: How to Teach Your Child Measurement and Unit Conversion.

acts.name: Angle Freeze Dance
acts.desc: Your child dances until you call an angle type: acute, right or obtuse. They freeze in a pose that shows that angle with their arms. If they're right, they call the next one. Add straight angles as confidence builds.

acts.name: Angle Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Acute is less than 90, right is exactly 90, obtuse is more than 90, straight is 180." Clap a beat and add an arm move for each type.

acts.name: Angle Spotter Art
acts.desc: Cut pictures with clear angles out of an old magazine. Your child glues them to a large sheet of paper, draws a small arc inside each angle and labels it acute, right or obtuse. Sorting real pictures builds the vocabulary before any protractor.

acts.name: Architect for a Day
acts.desc: Your child designs a building on graph paper with angle rules: the main hall has only right angles, and the roof meets at the top in an acute angle. They draw and label each part. The rules make angle types feel like real tools.

acts.name: Home Angle Hunt
acts.desc: Walk through one room and find examples of each angle type. The corner of a window is a right angle. A door opened partway makes an acute or obtuse angle with the wall, depending on how far it's open. Write down each example and its type.

acts.name: Sidewalk Angle Drawing
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw a circle and mark the center. Your child draws lines out from the center and estimates the angle between each pair, then measures with a protractor to check. Estimating first builds judgment that matters as much as reading the tool. If you don't have outdoor space, draw a large circle on paper on the floor.

acts.name: Protractor Practice
acts.desc: Draw five angles on paper ahead of time. Your child measures each with a protractor and writes the measurement and type. Then call out a measurement, like 45 degrees, and they draw it. Going back and forth between measuring and drawing builds real protractor skill.

focused.name: Angle Building
focused.desc: Stretch rubber bands to make an acute angle, then an obtuse angle, then a right angle. Ask, "Can you build a straight angle? What would it look like?" Measure each one with a protractor after building it. Use this early in the concept when building is still grounding the vocabulary.

focused.name: Angles Around a Point
focused.desc: Ask your child to fit green triangles around one point until they close the circle. Six fit, and a full turn is 360 degrees, so each corner is 360 ÷ 6 = 60 degrees. Repeat with the orange squares and the blue rhombuses to find their angles, then check one with a protractor. This is the mastery activity: finding an angle by dividing or adding parts of a full turn means your child understands angles as measures, not just shapes.

books.title: Sir Cumference and the Great Knight of Angleland
books.author: Cindy Neuschwander

clicking.signs: Your child looks at an angle and says "a bit more than 90, so obtuse" before measuring. Their protractor reading matches their estimate.
clicking.mixup: Reading a 60-degree angle as 120. The protractor has two rows of numbers and both look right, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Before reading the protractor, ask, "Is this angle smaller or bigger than a right angle?" Then pick the number that matches. Check against the corner of a book.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days finding right angles around the house and building them on the geoboard before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Measurement and Unit Conversion
opening: Converting units isn't memorizing rules. It's knowing that the same length can be described in different units, and that switching means knowing how many small units fit in a big one. Twelve inches fit in a foot, and 100 centimeters fit in a meter.
Once those relationships feel concrete, conversions stop being tricks to remember.
concepts.before: Your child should measure length and weight with the right tools and pick a sensible unit. If that still feels uncertain, spend time on Grade 3, Concept 9 first. Conversions built on shaky measuring produce correct-looking steps with nothing underneath.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child how many inches are in a foot by counting the inch marks on a ruler. Then line up three rulers along a tape measure to find how many feet make a yard.
concepts.next: When your child can convert between units and explain why the number changes when the unit changes, they are ready for Concept 10: How to Teach Your Child Multi-Step Problem Solving.

acts.name: Conversion Jump
acts.desc: Call out a conversion like "How many inches in 2 feet?" Your child works out 24, then jumps that many times while counting. For bigger numbers, stomp once for each ten and jump the rest. The movement makes the size of the change something they feel.

acts.name: Measurement Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant for key conversions: "Twelve inches in a foot, three feet in a yard, a hundred centimeters in a meter, a thousand grams in a kilo." Clap a beat and let your child add a line.

acts.name: Unit Comparison Art
acts.desc: On a long sheet of paper, your child draws a line 1 yard long with a tape measure, marks the 3 feet on it, then marks the 12 inches in the first foot. Underneath, they draw 1 meter and mark every 10 centimeters. Hang it up as a reference chart they made themselves.

acts.name: Home Contractor
acts.desc: Your child measures the length of one room in feet before pretend new flooring goes in. Then they convert to inches for the flooring company. Ask, "Which number is bigger? Why?"

acts.name: Recipe Conversions
acts.desc: Find a recipe that uses pounds and ounces and ask your child to rewrite it in ounces only. If it calls for 1/2 pound of butter and 4 ounces of chocolate, how many ounces is that altogether? The kitchen is full of real conversions.

acts.name: Measurement Walk
acts.desc: Outside, measure the length of the car in feet, then convert to inches. Measure a path in meters, then convert to centimeters. Estimate first each time. If you don't have outdoor space, measure a hallway instead.

acts.name: Conversion Challenge
acts.desc: Write a few problems that need a conversion before comparing. "One rope is 4 feet 6 inches. Another is 58 inches. Which is longer?" Your child decides which unit to change into. That choice matters as much as the math.

focused.name: Two Units Table
focused.desc: Set out a few objects and ask your child to measure each one in two units, like inches and feet or centimeters and meters, recording both in a table. Ask, "Which unit is more useful for this object? Why?" The length stays the same while the number changes. Use this early in the concept when using the tool and seeing the relationship still go together.

focused.name: Roll and Convert
focused.desc: Roll a number die for an amount of feet, like 4, and have your child convert it to inches. Roll again for meters and convert to centimeters. Then roll two dice for a mixed measurement, like 3 feet 5 inches, and convert it to inches only. This is the mastery activity: converting any amount without looking anything up means the unit relationships are truly known.

clicking.signs: Your child converts 3 feet to 36 inches and can explain why the number got bigger. They know a smaller unit always takes more of itself.
clicking.mixup: Dividing to turn 3 feet into inches and getting 1/4. Changing units feels like it should make things smaller, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Lay three rulers end to end. Ask, "How many inch marks did we pass?" Count by 12s together. Going from a big unit to a small one always means more of them.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days measuring and estimating (Grade 3, Concept 9) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Multi-Step Problem Solving
opening: A multi-step problem needs more than one calculation. The challenge isn't the math itself. It's reading carefully enough to know what's being asked and deciding which steps to take in which order.
Checking whether the answer makes sense is the step most kids skip. These are habits, and they grow through real situations.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable with all four operations and solve one-step word problems reliably. If one-step problems still need a lot of support, spend more time there first. Multi-step problems add planning on top of the math, so the math itself needs to be solid.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child: "You have $20. You buy a book for $7.50 and a snack for $2.25. How much is left?" Watch whether they find both steps and check the answer.
concepts.next: This completes the Grade 4 math core. Your child is ready for Grade 5, where decimals and fractions with different bottom numbers build on everything here.

acts.name: Problem Stomp
acts.desc: Read a multi-step problem aloud. Your child stomps once for each step they hear before solving anything. "We baked 48 cookies. We gave 12 to the neighbors and ate 6. How many are left?" Two stomps, then solve in that order.

acts.name: Problem Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Read it twice, find the steps, solve in order, check it makes sense." Clap a rhythm before each session. Putting the check in the chant makes it a required step, not an afterthought.

acts.name: Problem Illustration
acts.desc: Give your child a multi-step problem and ask them to draw it before calculating, one section of the page per step. For the cookie problem: 48 cookies, then 12 leaving, then 6 eaten. They solve from the drawing, then check with numbers.

acts.name: Problem Writers
acts.desc: Swap roles: your child writes a multi-step problem for you and works out the answer first. Solve it wrong on purpose so they have to explain where your thinking went off track. Writing a problem is harder than solving one.

acts.name: Shopping Trip Math
acts.desc: Next time you shop, give your child a budget and a short list. "We have $15 for snacks. Do we have enough for everything, and how much will be left?" Real money makes the steps feel worth doing.

acts.name: Sidewalk Problem Solving
acts.desc: With chalk outside, write a multi-step problem and draw a separate box for each step. Your child labels each box with what they're finding, then solves. Separate boxes make it easy to spot where an error happened. If you don't have outdoor space, use a large sheet of paper on the floor.

acts.name: Estimation First
acts.desc: Before solving any multi-step problem, your child rounds the numbers and estimates the answer in their head. Then they solve it exactly and compare. If the two are far apart, something went wrong. Estimating first is the best tool for catching errors.

focused.name: Step by Step
focused.desc: Write a story with several parts that add up, like "We picked 3 apples, then 4 more, then 2 more." Your child hangs a weight for each part on the left, one step at a time, and finds the single weight on the right that balances them all: 9. Then change one part of the story and ask what must change on the right. Use this early in the concept when acting out the steps is still needed.

focused.name: Bar Models
focused.desc: Build each amount in a problem as a cube train, with one cube standing for 10. "A class collected 60 cans on Monday and 40 on Tuesday. They need 150. How many more?" Your child builds 6 cubes and 4 cubes, then a 15-cube train for the goal, and lines them up to see the gap: 5 cubes, or 50 cans. This is the mastery activity: building a model before calculating means your child plans the steps instead of grabbing the first numbers they see.

clicking.signs: Your child names every step before calculating anything. When an answer seems too big or too small, they go back and check without being asked.
clicking.mixup: Adding every number in the story, like 48 + 12 + 6 = 66 cookies left. Numbers in a story feel like they should be added, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Act out a smaller version with crackers: start with 10, give 3 away, eat 2. Ask, "Did the pile get bigger or smaller?" Then match each action to an operation.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on one-step multiplication and division stories (Grade 3, Concepts 2 and 3) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Place Value with Decimals (to Thousandths)
opening: Place value is about position. A digit's position in a number decides what it is worth. Move it one place to the right and it becomes ten times smaller. Move it left and it becomes ten times larger. Decimals are the places to the right of the ones place.
Place value with decimals turns a number like 3.847 into something your child can read and reason about. It clicks through real numbers in real places, not drills.
concepts.before: Your child should already understand place value with whole numbers and know that a digit's position decides its value. If that still feels uncertain, spend time with whole number place value first. Skipping that step makes decimal work harder than it needs to be.
concepts.quickwin: Find a receipt or food label in your kitchen and ask your child to read the price or weight out loud, then tell you what the digit in the tenths place means.
concepts.next: When your child can read any decimal to the thousandths place, write it in a place value chart and explain what each digit is worth without hesitating, they are ready for Concept 2: How to Teach Your Child to Add and Subtract Fractions with Unlike Denominators.

acts.name: Decimal Dance
acts.desc: Call out a decimal number and give each place a move: stomp for ones, clap for tenths, jump for hundredths, spin for thousandths. Say "3.472" and your child stomps three times, claps four times, jumps seven times and spins twice. Switch roles so your child calls the number and you do the moves. Getting the order wrong is half the fun and most of the learning.

acts.name: Place Value Chant
acts.desc: Make up a simple chant together: "Ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths, that's the decimal way." Clap a beat while you say it, then try it backwards, from thousandths to ones. Let your child add a hand motion for each place. The rhythm builds the place names before any reading or writing.

acts.name: Place Value Art
acts.desc: Give your child a sheet of paper and a ruler. Ask them to draw four columns and label them ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths. Call out a decimal number and have them write each digit in its column, using a different color for each place. When the page is full, the colors show at a glance which place each digit belongs to.

acts.name: Playdough Place Value
acts.desc: Roll four small playdough balls and line them up on the table. Label four index cards ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and put one card in front of each ball. Call out a number like 2.364 and ask your child to press the right number of marks into each ball with a toothpick. The careful pressing gives every digit real attention.

acts.name: Grocery Store Decimals
acts.desc: Next time you're at the store or looking at a receipt together, point to a price and ask your child what each digit means. "$4.82 means 4 whole dollars, 8 dimes and 2 pennies." Tenths are dimes and hundredths are pennies. Real prices make the place names stick far better than made-up numbers.

acts.name: Sidewalk Decimal Number Line
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw a long number line. Mark 0 at one end and 1 at the other. Ask your child to place 0.5 first, then 0.25, then 0.1, then 0.75. Once those feel solid, add numbers to the hundredths and thousandths. Standing on the line shows that every decimal has its own spot between 0 and 1. If you don't have outdoor space, use masking tape on the floor indoors.

acts.name: Kitchen Scale Hunt
acts.desc: Switch a kitchen scale to kilograms and weigh a few things together, like an apple or a bag of rice. A reading like 0.368 kg goes all the way to thousandths. Ask your child to read each weight aloud. "What is the 3 worth? What about the 8?" Save this one for when the earlier activities feel easy, because thousandths are the hardest place to picture.

focused.name: Place Value Flip
focused.desc: Take out the face cards and let the tens stand for zero. Flip four cards and build a decimal number together, like 3.507. Ask your child to read it aloud and write it in a place value chart on paper. Then ask for the largest number they can make with the same four cards, and the smallest. The cards pick the digits, so nobody has to make up numbers. Use this early in the concept while the place names are still new.

focused.name: Decimal Compare
focused.desc: Lay out discs to build two decimal numbers side by side. Ask your child to read each one aloud and name the place of every digit. Then ask which number is larger and why. If you disagree, line the disc columns up and compare place by place, starting from the left. This is the mastery activity: your child has to explain which number is larger, not just say it, and the discs give them a way to check.

clicking.signs: Your child reads 4.307 as "four and three hundred seven thousandths" without pointing at each place. They tell you 0.5 is bigger than 0.25, and can say why: 5 tenths beats 2 tenths.
clicking.mixup: "0.25 is bigger than 0.5, because 25 is bigger than 5." Longer looks bigger, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Skip "no, that's wrong." Ask, "Would you rather have half a dollar or a quarter?" Then write both numbers in the place value chart and compare from the left, one place at a time.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on whole number place value (Grade 4, Concept 1) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Add and Subtract Fractions with Unlike Denominators
concepts.short: Add & Subtract Fractions with Unlike Denominators
opening: You can only add or subtract fractions when the pieces are the same size. The bottom number, the denominator, tells you the size. Before two fractions can be combined, they need to be changed into same-size pieces. Finding that common denominator is the whole skill.
The stumbling block is almost always the same: kids add the bottom numbers along with the top ones. Once your child sees why the pieces have to match first, the rest follows.
concepts.before: Your child should be able to find equivalent fractions and list multiples of a number without hesitating. If either of those feels shaky, spend time there first. Rushing into unlike denominators without that base makes everything harder to hold onto.
concepts.quickwin: Cut one strip of paper into 2 equal pieces and another into 4 equal pieces. Ask your child to add one piece from each strip and show you the answer using the strips, not numbers.
concepts.next: When your child can add and subtract two fractions with unlike denominators and explain why the denominators need to match first, they are ready for Concept 3: How to Teach Your Child to Multiply Fractions.

acts.name: Fraction Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Make the pieces match, then add the tops, the bottom stays the same." Clap a beat and let your child swap out words or add a stomp between lines. Run through it before any fraction activity that day. Saying the steps before doing them builds confidence.

acts.name: Paper Strip Fractions
acts.desc: Cut paper strips into equal sections: one into 2 pieces for halves, one into 4 for fourths, one into 3 for thirds. Lay them next to each other and ask your child to add 1/2 and 1/4 by lining up the strips. They can see that 1/2 is the same as 2/4, which makes the adding possible. This is the easiest starting point because the answer is visible before any calculating.

acts.name: Playdough Fraction Bars
acts.desc: Roll playdough into bars of the same length and cut them into fractions with a plastic knife. Make one bar in thirds and another in sixths. Ask your child to add 1/3 and 1/6 by lining the pieces up side by side. They find that 1/3 is the same as 2/6 just by looking. Let them build the answer in playdough before writing anything down.

acts.name: Fraction Number Line Art
acts.desc: Draw a long number line from 0 to 1 on paper. Ask your child to mark and label thirds in red, fourths in blue and sixths in green. When it's done, use it to add by counting forward and subtract by counting back. Wherever two colors land on the same mark, those fractions are equal, which shows the common denominator. Keep the line as a reference for the rest of the concept.

acts.name: Kitchen Fractions
acts.desc: Measuring cups are the best fraction tool in your house. Pour 1/3 cup of water into a clear glass, then add 1/4 cup. Ask your child how much water is in the glass now. Work out the common denominator on paper together, then pour the water into a measuring cup to check. Use water so nothing goes to waste.

acts.name: Fraction Story Walk
acts.desc: Walk around the block and make up a fraction story as you go. "We walked 1/2 a block to the corner, then 1/4 of a block to the mailbox. How far have we walked altogether?" Add to the story at each landmark. Your child works out each problem out loud as you walk. This is harder than the kitchen activity because there is nothing to pour and check.

acts.name: Fraction Freeze
acts.desc: Write a few fractions on index cards and spread them on the floor. Play music and dance. When you stop the music, call out an addition or subtraction problem using two of the cards. Your child finds both cards and works out the answer while everyone stays frozen, taking as long as they need. Then they pick the next dance move. This is the hardest daily activity because your child has to find the common denominator with no strips or bars to look at.

focused.name: Fraction Building
focused.tool: Fraction Tower Cubes by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Snap together cubes to build two fractions with unlike denominators, like 1/2 and 1/3. Ask your child to find a cube size that fits both towers evenly. Then rebuild both fractions in that size and add them by counting the pieces. Snapping the pieces together shows equivalent fractions without any drawing or writing. Use this early in the concept while seeing the pieces still matters most.

focused.name: Fill the Tube
focused.tool: Fraction Formula Game by Educational Insights
focused.desc: Play a round together. Each time your child adds a fraction piece to a tube, they say the new total out loud, like 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, before checking it against the pieces. This is the mastery activity: the game hands out pieces of different sizes, so your child has to find a common denominator on every turn.

books.title: Full House: An Invitation to Fractions
books.author: Dayle Ann Dodds

clicking.signs: Your child changes 1/2 + 1/3 into sixths before adding, without a reminder. They can tell you 2/5 can't be right, because the answer has to be bigger than 1/2.
clicking.mixup: "1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5." Adding the bottom numbers feels as natural as adding the top ones, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Lay a half strip and a third strip end to end and ask, "Two pieces of what?" Then find the piece size that fits both evenly, swap each strip for those pieces, and add.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on equivalent fractions (Grade 4, Concept 5) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Multiply Fractions
opening: Multiplying fractions means finding a part of a part. When you multiply 1/2 by 1/4, you are asking: what is half of one quarter? The answer gets smaller because you are taking a piece of a piece.
Top times top, bottom times bottom. That is the whole procedure, and it is simpler than most kids expect once they see what it means. Start with real objects before moving to numbers on paper.
concepts.before: Your child should know what a fraction means and be able to multiply whole numbers without hesitating. If either feels uncertain, spend time there first. The activities here depend on your child already having a clear picture of what one fraction looks like.
concepts.quickwin: Cut a piece of paper in half, then fold one of those halves in half again. Ask your child what fraction of the whole paper they are holding.
concepts.next: When your child can multiply two fractions and explain why the answer is smaller than either fraction they started with, they are ready for Concept 4: How to Teach Your Child to Divide Fractions.

acts.name: Fraction Multiplication Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Top times top, bottom times bottom, simplify if you can." Clap a rhythm and let your child change the words or add a stomp between lines. Run through it before any fraction multiplication that day. Hearing the steps first makes them easier to follow later.

acts.name: Fraction of a Snack
acts.desc: Put 12 grapes, crackers or blueberries on the table. Ask your child to take half. Then ask them to take half of what they are holding. "What fraction of the whole pile do you have now?" Let them count to check: 3 out of 12 is 1/4. Then write it together as 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. This is the easiest activity because the answer can be counted.

acts.name: Playdough Portions
acts.desc: Roll out a flat playdough circle as the whole. Ask your child to cut it into thirds with a plastic knife, then take one third and cut it in half. "What part of the whole circle is this piece?" Try it with other fractions. Watching the piece shrink shows the key idea: multiplying two fractions gives you less than you started with.

acts.name: Fraction Strips Art
acts.desc: Give your child a strip of paper and two colors. Ask them to color 3/4 of the strip red, then color half of the red part blue. Ask, "What fraction of the whole strip is blue?" The overlap shows the answer, 3/8, before anything is written. Fold the strip into eighths to check.

acts.name: Recipe Helper
acts.desc: Pull out a simple recipe and cut it in half together. If the recipe calls for 3/4 cup of flour and you are making half, how much do you need? Work it out on paper first. Then pull out the measuring cups and ask, "Do we have a 3/8 cup? No, so how do we measure it?" Your child figures out that 1/4 cup plus half of a 1/4 cup gets them there. Solving a real problem with no perfect tool is a better lesson than any textbook example.

acts.name: Sticky Note Fractions
acts.desc: Write numbers 1 to 8 on sticky notes and spread them across a table. Call out a problem like "half of three quarters." Your child picks the notes to build 1/2 × 3/4, then multiplies across: top times top, bottom times bottom. Swap roles so your child calls the problem and you build it.

acts.name: Chalk Fractions
acts.desc: Draw a large rectangle on the pavement with chalk. Ask your child to divide it into four equal parts and color three of them. Then, with a different color, shade half of one of those parts. Ask, "What fraction of the whole rectangle is that small section?" This is the hardest daily activity because your child has to picture the pieces without objects to count. Use a large sheet of paper indoors if needed.

focused.name: Part of a Part
focused.desc: Lay out three 1/4 tiles to show 3/4. Ask your child to find half of it. They swap the fourths for eighths, see that 3/4 is the same as 6/8, and take half: 3/8. Then try half of 2/3 and a third of 1/2. Use this early in the concept while your child still needs to see the pieces.

focused.name: Fraction War
focused.desc: Each player flips two fraction cards and multiplies them. The larger product takes all four cards. When you disagree about which is larger, sketch both products on paper before deciding. This is the mastery activity: your child multiplies, then has to judge which product is bigger, which only works if they know what the answer means.

books.title: Full House: An Invitation to Fractions
books.author: Dayle Ann Dodds

books.title: The Hershey's Milk Chocolate Fractions Book
books.author: Jerry Pallotta

clicking.signs: Your child reads 1/2 × 1/4 as "half of a quarter" and predicts a smaller answer before working it out. They can fold paper to show why 1/2 × 1/3 is 1/6.
clicking.mixup: "Multiplying makes numbers bigger, so 1/2 × 1/4 can't be 1/8." That is true for whole numbers, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Fold a sheet of paper into quarters and shade one. Fold that quarter in half and ask, "What is half of a quarter?" Count how many of the small pieces fill the whole sheet.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on multiplying fractions by whole numbers (Grade 4, Concept 7) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Divide Fractions
opening: Dividing by a fraction asks, "How many of these fit inside that?" When you divide 2 by 1/4, you are asking how many quarter pieces fit inside 2 wholes. The answer is 8, which is bigger than what you started with. That is the surprise: dividing by a fraction makes the answer larger.

In 5th grade this means two kinds of problems: a unit fraction divided by a whole number, and a whole number divided by a unit fraction. A unit fraction has a 1 on top, like 1/3. Staying inside those two kinds keeps this concept manageable.
concepts.before: Your child should be able to multiply fractions with confidence and know what a unit fraction is. If multiplying fractions still feels uncertain, go back to Concept 3 for a week first. Knowing how multiplying works is what makes dividing make sense.
concepts.quickwin: Put 1/2 a cup of water in a glass. Ask your child how many 1/4 cup portions fit inside it. Pour and count together to check.
concepts.next: When your child can divide a unit fraction by a whole number and a whole number by a unit fraction, and explain why the answers move in opposite directions, they are ready for Concept 5: How to Teach Your Child to Add and Subtract Decimals.

acts.name: Division Chant
acts.desc: Make up a short chant for each kind of problem. For a whole number divided by a unit fraction: "How many fit inside? Count them up." For a unit fraction divided by a whole number: "Split the piece, make it smaller." Clap a beat while saying both, and let your child pick which chant fits a problem before solving it. Naming the kind of problem is half the work.

acts.name: Kitchen Cups
acts.desc: Use measuring cups and a clear glass. Pour 1 cup of water and ask your child how many 1/4 cup portions fit inside. Pour and count together. Then try 2 cups divided by 1/3, using a pitcher for the larger amount. The pouring gives the answer before anything is written. This is the easiest activity because you can see and count every portion.

acts.name: Paper Folding Fractions
acts.desc: Fold a strip of paper to show 1/2. Ask, "If we split this half into 2 equal pieces, what is each piece?" Your child folds the half in half again and sees 1/4. Next, lightly mark another strip into thirds. Your child folds one third into 3 equal pieces. Each tiny piece is 1/9 of the whole strip. Keep the strips to use as a reference.

acts.name: Playdough Division
acts.desc: Roll a playdough strip as one whole and cut it into thirds with a plastic knife. Ask, "How many thirds fit in 3 wholes?" Roll two more strips of the same length, cut them into thirds and line all three up. Count the thirds together: 9. Your child can see how many pieces fit inside before any math is written.

acts.name: Fraction Bar Map
acts.desc: Give your child a strip of paper, a ruler and two colors. Ask them to draw a bar for 1 whole and split it into fourths in one color. Then split one of those fourths in half with the second color. Label every section. One page now shows both kinds of problems: how many fourths fit in the whole, and what you get when one fourth is split.

acts.name: Division Story Walk
acts.desc: Walk around the block and make up division problems about what you see. "There are 3 flower beds. If we split each one into quarters, how many quarter-beds is that?" At the next stop: "Each fence panel is 1/4 of the fence. If we split one panel into 2 equal parts, what fraction of the fence is each part?" Add a new problem at each thing you pass.

acts.name: Tape Line Steps
acts.desc: Stick a long strip of painter's tape on the floor to stand for one whole and mark it into quarters. Ask, "How many quarters fit in 2 wholes?" Your child walks the strip twice in quarter steps and counts: 8. Then ask, "If we split one quarter between 2 people, how big is each part?" Your child finds the middle of one quarter and names the piece: 1/8. This is the hardest daily activity because it mixes both kinds of problems with nothing written down.

focused.name: Fraction Building
focused.tool: Fraction Tower Cubes by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Snap together whole towers to show a whole number, like 2. Ask your child how many 1/3 pieces fit alongside them, and count. Then take one 1/3 piece and find the smaller pieces that split it into 2 equal parts. Use this early in the concept while seeing the pieces still matters.

focused.name: Rod Division
focused.desc: Let the orange rod be one whole. The red rod is 1/5 of it. Ask, "How many fifths fit in 2 wholes?" Your child lines red rods along two orange rods and counts 10. Then ask, "What is 1/5 split into 2 equal parts?" Two white rods match one red rod, and each white rod is 1/10 of the whole. Finally, your child makes up one problem of each kind for you to build. This is the mastery activity: making up problems shows your child knows which kind is which.

books.title: Full House: An Invitation to Fractions
books.author: Dayle Ann Dodds

clicking.signs: Your child reads 2 ÷ 1/4 as "how many quarters fit in 2" and gets 8. They can also tell you that 1/4 ÷ 2 means sharing a quarter between 2 people, so the answer is 1/8.
clicking.mixup: "2 ÷ 1/4 is 1/2, because dividing makes things smaller." With whole numbers it always does, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Pull out the measuring cups. Ask, "How many quarter cups of water fill 2 cups?" and pour to check. Getting 8 from a division makes the bigger answer real.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a week on Concept 3: Multiply Fractions before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Add and Subtract Decimals
opening: Adding and subtracting decimals works the same way as whole numbers, with one rule that never bends: line up the decimal points before you start. Lining up the points keeps tenths with tenths and hundredths with hundredths. Skip that step and the digits land in the wrong places.
Once your child understands why the rule exists, the adding itself is straightforward. The real work here is building the habit of lining up first.
concepts.before: Your child should be able to read and write decimals to the thousandths place and know what each digit is worth. If that still feels uncertain, go back to Concept 1 first. Without it, lining up the points is just a step to memorize instead of a step that makes sense.
concepts.quickwin: Find two prices on a grocery receipt and ask your child to add them together on paper. Watch whether they line up the decimal points before adding. That one habit is the whole lesson.
concepts.next: When your child lines up the decimal points without being reminded and gets addition and subtraction right every time, they are ready for Concept 6: How to Teach Your Child to Multiply and Divide Decimals.

acts.name: Decimal Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Line up the points before you start, tenths with tenths, that's the smart part." Clap a rhythm and let your child add a move between lines. Run through it before any decimal activity that day. Saying the rule out loud builds the habit better than reminders after mistakes.

acts.name: Receipt Math
acts.desc: Pull out a grocery receipt or print one from a recent online order. Ask your child to pick two items and add the prices on paper. Then subtract one price from the total. Check the answer together against the receipt. This is the easiest activity because the decimal points are already printed and the answer is easy to check.

acts.name: Ruler Decimals
acts.desc: Pull out a ruler marked in centimeters and millimeters. Ask your child to add two lengths: "This pencil is 14.3 cm and this eraser is 5.7 cm. How long are they end to end?" Then subtract: "If we cut 3.8 cm off the pencil, how long is it now?" The ruler gives real decimal numbers, and every answer can be checked by measuring.

acts.name: Decimal Color Grid Art
acts.desc: Draw a 10 by 10 grid on paper and tell your child the whole grid equals 1. Ask them to shade 0.36 in one color and 0.45 in another. Count all the shaded squares together and write the answer as a decimal. Then try subtracting: shade 0.72 and cross out 0.38 of those squares. Your child watches the answer appear as they count.

acts.name: Playdough Decimal Mats
acts.desc: Roll thin playdough ropes and shape the digits of two decimal numbers on the table, one above the other. Use a small ball of playdough as the decimal point in each number. Ask your child to slide the numbers until the two balls line up. Then solve the problem on paper. Lining up the balls with their hands makes the rule feel real.

acts.name: Decimal Story Walk
acts.desc: Walk around the block and make up a money story about what you see. "That garden has $12.45 worth of tomatoes and $3.28 worth of herbs. How much is that altogether?" At the next stop: "We walked 0.75 of a mile to the corner and 0.48 of a mile to the mailbox. How far have we gone?" Keep the numbers small and the story real.

acts.name: Decimal Point Stomp
acts.desc: Call out a problem like 3.5 + 2.25. Your child writes both numbers in the air with a finger, one above the other, lining up the points. Then they work from right to left, stomping once for each column and saying its name as they add it: hundredths, tenths, ones. Switch roles so your child calls the problem. This is the hardest daily activity because your child has to hold the lined-up numbers in their head.

focused.name: Decimal Place Value Building
focused.desc: Lay out discs for two decimal numbers, one above the other, with the place columns lined up. Add the discs column by column from right to left, trading ten small discs for one bigger disc whenever a column reaches ten. The trading step is where most mistakes happen, and the discs make it visible. Use this early in the concept while the hands-on support matters most.

focused.name: Coin Totals
focused.desc: Play a round together. Each time your child collects coins, they write the amount in dollars and cents, like $1.35, and add it to their running total with the decimal points lined up. Count the coins to check the written total. This is the mastery activity: lining up the points comes up on every turn, so the habit becomes automatic.

books.title: Alexander, Who Used to Be Rich Last Sunday
books.author: Judith Viorst

clicking.signs: Your child lines up the decimal points without a reminder and writes 4.2 as 4.20 on their own. They estimate "about 5 and a half" before working out 4.2 + 1.35.
clicking.mixup: "4.2 + 1.35 = 1.77." The digits get lined up on the right, the way whole numbers are, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Ask for an estimate before any writing. Then turn it into money: $4.20 plus $1.35. Write both amounts so the dots sit in one straight column and add from there.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on Concept 1: Place Value with Decimals before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Multiply and Divide Decimals
opening: Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1,000 shifts every digit to the left, so the number grows. Dividing by them shifts every digit to the right, so the number shrinks. It looks like the decimal point jumps around, but it follows the same rule every time.
Once your child sees the pattern, multiplying and dividing decimals becomes manageable. Building that feel with real objects first saves a lot of confusion later.
concepts.before: Your child should add and subtract decimals with confidence and understand place value to the thousandths. If either feels shaky, spend time with Concepts 1 and 5 first. The direction rule in this concept only makes sense when your child knows what each place is worth.
concepts.quickwin: Ask your child what 0.5 times 2 equals. Work it out together using two strips of paper that each show one half. The answer of 1 whole surprises most kids and opens the door to the concept.
concepts.next: When your child can multiply and divide decimals and predict which way the digits move, the decimal work is complete. Concept 7: How to Teach Your Child to Classify Two-Dimensional Figures starts something new: a break from numbers to look closely at shapes.

acts.name: Place Value Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Times ten, the digits slide left. Divide by ten, they slide right." Clap a beat and let your child add a hand motion for sliding each way. Run through it before any decimal multiplying or dividing that day. The direction is the hardest part of this concept, and saying it out loud builds the habit.

acts.name: Playdough Decimal Strips
acts.desc: Tell your child that 10 cm stands for one whole. Roll three playdough strips, each 3 cm long, and label each one 0.3. Line them up end to end and measure: 9 cm, or 0.9. Then cut one strip into two equal pieces and ask what each piece is worth. This is the easiest activity because the answer can be measured before anything is calculated.

acts.name: Decimal Point Jump
acts.desc: Write a decimal number in large digits across a row of sticky notes on the wall, with the point on its own note. Call out "times 10" and have your child move the point note one place to the right. For "times 100," two places. For dividing, move it left. Read the new number aloud each time. Switch roles so your child calls the operation and you move the point.

acts.name: Receipt Multiplication
acts.desc: Pull out a grocery receipt and pick one item. Ask, "If we bought 3 of these, how much would it cost?" Multiply the price by the whole number on paper. Then divide a total by the number of items to find the price of one. Keep the multipliers between 2 and 9 so the focus stays on the decimal point.

acts.name: Decimal Tile Art
acts.desc: Draw a rectangle on paper and divide it into 10 equal columns. Shade 4 columns to show 0.4. Ask, "If we take 0.4 three times, how much do we have?" Draw and shade two more rectangles the same way and count the shaded columns: 12 tenths, or 1.2. Seeing the answer pass 1 makes it feel logical instead of surprising.

acts.name: Grocery Store Estimation Walk
acts.desc: Walk through a grocery store or look at a store flyer together. Pick an item with a decimal price and ask your child to estimate the cost of different amounts. "Apples are $1.25 each. About how much would 4 cost? What about 8?" Work out the exact answer after the estimate. Estimating first turns the written work into a check.

acts.name: Sidewalk Decimal Scaling
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw a line 1 meter long. Ask your child to mark 0.5 m, then 0.25 m, then 0.1 m along it. Ask, "If we made the 0.25 m piece 3 times longer, how long would it be?" Mark it out and measure: 0.75 m. Then ask, "If we split the whole line into 4 equal pieces, how long is each one?" This is the hardest daily activity because your child is working with decimals and measuring at the same time.

focused.name: Decimal Scaling
focused.desc: Lay out discs for a decimal number in place value columns. To multiply by 10, your child moves every disc one column to the left. To divide by 10, they move every disc one column to the right. Read the number aloud after each move. Use this early in the concept while moving the discs still helps the direction stick.

focused.name: Price Tag Shop
focused.tool: Pretend and Play Money by Learning Resources
focused.desc: Set up a small shop with price tags like $1.25 and $0.40. Your child buys 3 of one item, then splits a $4.80 bill evenly among 4 people. Before each problem, they predict whether the answer will be bigger or smaller than the price. Then they count out the money to check. This is the mastery activity: predicting first means the rule makes sense to them, not just the steps.

books.title: How Much, How Many, How Far, How Heavy, How Long, How Tall Is 1000?
books.author: Helen Nolan

clicking.signs: Before calculating, your child predicts whether the answer will be bigger or smaller. They get 2.5 × 10 = 25 and 2.5 ÷ 10 = 0.25, and say each digit moved one place.
clicking.mixup: "To multiply by 10, just add a zero, so 2.5 × 10 is 2.50." That trick works for whole numbers, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Make it money. Ask, "If one snack costs $2.50, what do 10 cost?" Your child knows it is not $2.50. Then show the digits sliding one place left on a place value chart.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on Concept 1: Place Value with Decimals before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child to Classify Two-Dimensional Figures
opening: Shapes belong to families, and one shape can belong to several at once. Every square is a rectangle. Every rectangle is a parallelogram. Every parallelogram is a quadrilateral. A shape doesn't stop being one thing when it becomes another, just like your child belongs to a family and a neighborhood at the same time.
The goal is not memorizing shape names. It is understanding why one shape fits more than one group.
concepts.before: Your child should know the names of common shapes and be able to spot parallel sides and right angles. If those feel uncertain, spend a few days noticing and naming shapes around the house first. Sorting shapes into families depends on that.
concepts.quickwin: Put a square piece of paper on the table and ask your child: "Is this a rectangle?" Most kids say no. Talk it through together. That one conversation is the heart of this whole concept.
concepts.next: When your child can look at any four-sided shape and list every group it belongs to without prompting, they are ready for Concept 8: How to Teach Your Child Volume of Rectangular Prisms.

acts.name: Shape Shake
acts.desc: Call out a shape feature and have your child strike a pose that shows it with their body. "Show me two parallel sides": they stretch both arms out straight. "Show me a right angle": they hold one arm straight out and one straight up. "Show me four equal sides": they make a square with their fingers. The sillier the poses the better. This works on one feature at a time before combining them.

acts.name: Shape Family Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Quadrilateral is the family name, parallelogram plays the same game, rectangles fit, squares do too, every square's a rectangle through and through." Clap a rhythm and let your child change the words or add stomps between lines. Run through it before any shape sorting that day.

acts.name: Shape Scavenger Hunt
acts.desc: Walk through your home and find real objects for different shape groups. A picture frame is a rectangle, which also makes it a parallelogram and a quadrilateral. A square tile belongs to all of those groups too. Write down each object and every group it belongs to. Real objects make the families feel natural.

acts.name: Sticky Note Shape Sort
acts.desc: Write these shape names on sticky notes: square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezoid, quadrilateral. Stick them on the wall and ask your child to arrange them from the biggest family at the top to the most specific at the bottom. Connect related ones with string or a drawn line. The notes move easily, so your child can change their mind without erasing.

acts.name: Playdough Shape Sorting
acts.desc: Roll playdough flat and cut out squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapezoids and rhombuses. Ask your child to sort them by feature. Which have two pairs of parallel sides? Which have four right angles? Which have four equal sides? Some shapes belong in more than one pile. Moving them between piles makes the overlap concrete.

acts.name: Outdoor Shape Walk
acts.desc: Walk outside and look for shapes on buildings, fences, sidewalks and signs. Each time you spot a four-sided shape, name every group it belongs to. A window is a rectangle, a parallelogram and a quadrilateral. A diamond-shaped road sign is a rhombus and a parallelogram. This is harder than the home hunt because the shapes appear without warning. If you can't get outside, look at pictures in books or magazines.

acts.name: Shape Sketch Book
acts.desc: Ask your child to draw the shape family tree from memory. Quadrilaterals go at the top, parallelograms branch below, then rectangles and rhombuses, then squares at the bottom where those two branches meet. Next to each shape, they write two features that put it in that spot. This is the hardest daily activity because there is nothing to look at or hold.

focused.name: Shape Classification
focused.desc: Lay out the blocks and ask your child to sort them by one feature at a time: number of sides, then right angles, then equal sides. Then sort by two features at once. Some blocks belong in two groups, which makes the overlap easy to see. Use this early in the concept while sorting by one feature is still the focus.

focused.name: Shape Building
focused.desc: Stretch rubber bands across the pegs to build four-sided shapes. Ask your child to build a shape that is both a rectangle and a rhombus. They discover that only a square fits. Then ask for a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. This is the mastery activity: your child has to build shapes that follow the rules, not just name them.

books.title: Sir Cumference and the First Round Table
books.author: Cindy Neuschwander

clicking.signs: Your child holds up a square and names every family it belongs to: quadrilateral, parallelogram, rectangle and rhombus. They can also tell you why a rectangle is not always a square.
clicking.mixup: "A square isn't a rectangle. Rectangles are long." Most rectangles kids see are long, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Skip the debate about names. Ask, "What does a shape need to be a rectangle?" Write the rules down: four sides, four right angles. Then check the square against each rule together.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on angles and shape features (Grade 4, Concept 8) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Volume of Rectangular Prisms
opening: Volume is how many unit cubes fill a box shape. To find it, count the cubes in one flat layer, then multiply by the number of layers. Length times width gives you one layer. Times the height gives you all the layers.
The formula is a shortcut for counting every cube. It only makes sense after your child has filled a box with cubes and counted them, so build first. The formula comes last.
concepts.before: Your child should understand the area of a rectangle and multiply two numbers without hesitating. Area is one layer of volume, and saying that out loud saves a lot of confusion later. If area still feels uncertain, spend time there first.
concepts.quickwin: Find a small rectangular box in your kitchen, like a tea box or a cracker box. Ask your child to guess how many sugar cubes or dice would fit inside. Count together to check. That guess and check is the whole concept in two minutes.
concepts.next: When your child can work out the volume of any rectangular prism with the formula and explain what each number stands for, they are ready for Concept 9: How to Teach Your Child the Coordinate Plane.

acts.name: Volume Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "Length times width gives you the floor, times the height and you have more." Clap a beat and let your child swap out words or add a jump between lines. Run through it before any volume activity that day.

acts.name: Kitchen Volume
acts.desc: Use a rectangular food storage container and a measuring cup. Ask your child to predict how many quarter-cup scoops of rice or dried beans will fill it. Fill it together and count the scoops. Filling and counting gives a feel for volume before the formula comes in. This is the easiest activity because the answer shows up as you fill.

acts.name: Sugar Cube Building
acts.desc: Use a box of sugar cubes or small wooden cubes. Ask your child to build a box shape 3 cubes long, 2 cubes wide and 2 cubes tall. Count the cubes. Then ask, "What is 3 times 2 times 2?" The count and the multiplication should match. Build another shape with different sizes and check again.

acts.name: Box Hunt
acts.desc: Collect four or five rectangular boxes of different sizes from your kitchen or pantry, like cereal, pasta, tea and tissue boxes. Ask your child to order them from smallest to largest volume before measuring anything. Then measure each side with a ruler and work out the actual volume. The gap between the guess and the answer is where the learning happens.

acts.name: Volume Freeze Dance
acts.desc: Play music and dance. When the music stops, call out three small numbers for length, width and height, between 2 and 6. Your child freezes and multiplies all three, taking as long as they need. When they have the answer, they pick the next dance move. This is harder than the building activities because there are no cubes to count.

acts.name: Chalk Box City
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw the outline of a few rectangular buildings and label each one with a length and width. Ask your child to work out the floor area of each building. Then give each one a height and work out its volume. Line the buildings up from smallest to largest volume. If you don't have outdoor space, draw the city on a large sheet of paper.

acts.name: Box Packing Challenge
acts.desc: Find a medium-sized box and a pile of same-sized small boxes or blocks. Ask your child to predict how many small boxes will fit inside. Pack them in layer by layer and count. Then work it out with the formula and compare. This is the hardest daily activity because your child has to explain any gap between the guess and the real count.

focused.name: Volume Building
focused.desc: Ask your child to build a box shape with snap cubes and write down its length, width and height. Then find the volume two ways: count every cube, and multiply the three numbers. The two answers should match every time. Use this early in the concept while your child is still connecting counting to the formula.

focused.name: Volume Puzzle
focused.desc: Play a puzzle together before your child tries one alone. Each puzzle fills a space with blocks of different shapes. After each one is solved, ask your child to work out the volume of the finished cube shape. This is the mastery activity: the odd-shaped pieces make your child think about volume without a neat grid of cubes to count.

books.title: How Tall, How Short, How Faraway?
books.author: David A. Adler

clicking.signs: Your child counts the cubes in one layer, then multiplies by the number of layers without being shown. They can explain that length times width is the bottom layer.
clicking.mixup: "A box 3 long, 2 wide and 2 tall holds 7 cubes, because 3 + 2 + 2 = 7." There are three numbers to combine, so adding them feels natural.
clicking.todo: Build it. Make the bottom layer with 6 cubes, then stack a second layer on top. Count all 12 together and ask, "Could 7 cubes fill this box?"
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days on area of rectangles (Grade 3, Concept 7) before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child the Coordinate Plane
opening: The coordinate plane is a map where every spot has a two-number address. The first number tells you how far to move right. The second tells you how far to move up. The order never changes: right first, up second. That rule is the whole concept.

Every point has exactly one address, written as two numbers in parentheses, like (3, 5). Once your child knows the order matters and that every trip starts from zero, plotting and reading points becomes straightforward.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable reading a number line from 0 to 10 or more. If number lines still feel uncertain, spend a few days building and reading them first. The coordinate plane is just two number lines that meet at zero.
concepts.quickwin: Draw a simple grid on paper with one point marked on it. Ask your child how far right and how far up the point is from the corner. That two-number answer is a coordinate pair, and they just found one.
concepts.next: When your child can plot any coordinate pair and read the coordinates of any point without reversing the order, they are ready for Concept 10: How to Teach Your Child Expressions and Equations.

acts.name: Coordinate Freeze Dance
acts.desc: Tape a simple grid on the floor with painter's tape, big enough to stand on. Call out a coordinate pair and have your child walk to that spot: right first, then up. When they land on it, they freeze and strike a pose. Call the next pair and they dance their way there. This is the easiest activity because the right-then-up movement happens with their whole body.

acts.name: Coordinate Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "First go right, then go up, x before y, never mix it up." Clap a rhythm and let your child add a move for each direction. Run through it before any coordinate activity that day. Mixing up the order is the most common mistake, and saying it out loud builds the habit early.

acts.name: Coordinate Scavenger Hunt
acts.desc: Before you start, hide four or five small objects around the room and draw a simple grid map that shows each one's coordinates. Give your child the map and ask them to find each object using only the coordinates. When they find one, they write its pair on paper before moving on.

acts.name: City Map Art
acts.desc: Give your child a sheet of graph paper and ask them to number the bottom and left edges, then draw a small city on the grid. Buildings and parks go at specific points. When the map is done, ask questions: "What is at (3, 5)? How do you get from (1, 2) to (4, 7)?" Their own map makes the addresses feel useful.

acts.name: Battleship on Paper
acts.desc: Draw two matching grids on paper, one for each player, and number both edges from 0 to 10. Each player secretly marks five points on their own grid. Take turns calling out coordinate pairs to find each other's points. Keep going until both players have found all five. No board game needed.

acts.name: Connect the Dots Coordinate Art
acts.desc: Give your child graph paper with numbered edges. Call out six to eight coordinate pairs and have them plot each point and connect them in order to reveal a simple shape. When they finish, ask them to read back each point's coordinates without looking at your list. This is harder than Battleship because every point has to be exact.

acts.name: Sidewalk Coordinate Grid
acts.desc: With chalk outside, draw a large grid on the pavement and number both edges. Call out pairs and have your child mark each point with a small rock. Connect the rocks in order and ask your child to name the shape. Then name a shape, like a square, and ask them to pick coordinates that make it. This is the hardest daily activity because your child works backward from the shape.

focused.name: Coordinate Plotting
focused.desc: Turn the geoboard into a grid by labeling the pegs along the bottom and left edges with numbers on small stickers. Call out coordinate pairs and have your child loop a rubber band on each peg. Connect several points to make a shape, then ask your child to name it and list the coordinates of each corner. Use this early in the concept while the right-then-up steps are still new.

focused.name: Copy My Picture
focused.tool: XY Coordinate Grid Whiteboards by hand2mind
focused.desc: Sit back to back, each with a grid board. Your child draws a simple picture by connecting points, then reads out the coordinates one at a time while you plot them on your own board. Compare the two pictures. If they don't match, find the pair that got flipped. Then switch roles. This is the mastery activity: the picture only comes out right if every pair is read and plotted in the right order.

clicking.signs: Your child plots (3, 5) and (5, 3) in two different places and can tell you why. They read a point's address by starting at zero every time.
clicking.mixup: Plotting (3, 5) as up 3 and over 5. Both numbers look equal, so the order seems not to matter.
clicking.todo: Use a short phrase: "Walk before you climb." Your child walks right along the bottom first, then climbs up. Mark (3, 5) and (5, 3) on the same grid so they see two different spots.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days building and reading number lines before moving on.

concepts.title: How to Teach Your Child Expressions and Equations
opening: An expression is a math phrase that describes a situation. A variable is a letter that stands for a number you don't know yet. When you write n + 3, you are saying "some number plus three." You are not solving anything. You are describing.
That shift from calculating to describing is what makes this concept feel new. In 5th grade, the goal is to read and write math the way you read and write sentences.
concepts.before: Your child should be comfortable with all four operations. Letters standing for numbers are new here, so start with a blank box or a question mark, like ? + 3, before switching to letters. That small step heads off a lot of confusion.
concepts.quickwin: Put some apples on the table and say: "I have some apples and I add 3 more. How would you write that in math without knowing how many I started with?" Let your child work it out. That one question is the whole concept in a single moment.
concepts.next: When your child can read a real-life situation and write the matching expression without help, and explain the difference between an expression and an equation, they have completed the 5th grade math core. 6th grade builds directly from here.

acts.name: Expression Chant
acts.desc: Make up a chant together: "An expression tells the story. An equation says two sides are the same." Clap a rhythm and let your child add a hand motion for each line. The difference between an expression and an equation is the most important idea in this concept.

acts.name: Kitchen Expression Builder
acts.desc: Cook or bake something simple together and turn steps into expressions, using a letter for anything you haven't counted. "We have some eggs and we use 2" becomes e − 2. "We split the batter evenly into 12 muffin cups" becomes b ÷ 12. Write each expression on a sticky note and line them up in order. This is the easiest activity because the situation is right in front of you.

acts.name: Story to Expression
acts.desc: Read a few sentences from any book together. Stop wherever an amount is unknown and ask your child to write an expression for it. "The farmer had some chickens and bought 6 more" becomes n + 6. "She split her savings evenly into 3 jars" becomes n ÷ 3. Any story works. The skill is spotting the math hidden in the words.

acts.name: Expression Art
acts.desc: Ask your child to draw four expressions as pictures. n + 5 might be a bag of marbles you can't see inside, next to 5 loose ones. 3 × n might be three equal bags. Label each picture with its expression. Drawing it shows which part is known and which part is unknown.

acts.name: Expression Scavenger Hunt
acts.desc: Write four or five expressions on index cards and hide them around the room. Give your child a matching story card for each one and ask them to find its expression. "You save the same amount every week. How much after 4 weeks?" matches 4 × n. Matching connects words and symbols without any writing.

acts.name: Expression Freeze Dance
acts.desc: Call out a real-life story. Your child acts it out, freezes and writes the expression on paper. "You have some stickers and you get 5 more": they act out getting stickers, freeze and write n + 5. "You share your cards evenly among 4 friends": they mime dealing cards, freeze and write n ÷ 4. This is harder than matching because your child writes the expression on their own.

acts.name: Sidewalk Expression Story
acts.desc: With chalk outside, write expressions at different spots on the pavement. Walk to each one together. Your child makes up a story that fits and writes it next to the expression. n + 4 might become "I found some shells and picked up 4 more." This is the hardest daily activity because it goes the other way, from symbols back to a story. Use index cards on the floor if you can't get outside.

focused.name: Mystery Cup
focused.desc: Turn a paper cup upside down and hide some cubes under it. The cup is n. Put 5 loose cubes next to it and ask your child to write the expression: n + 5. Build a few more, like two cups with the same hidden amount, which is 2 × n. Then lift the cups, count, and work out the value. Use this early in the concept while seeing the unknown still helps.

focused.name: Balance the Pawns
focused.desc: Set up the balance picture with pawns standing for the unknown and number cubes for known amounts, like two pawns and a 3 on one side and an 11 on the other. Your child writes the equation, 2 × n + 3 = 11, and then tells a story that matches it. Only then do they work out what each pawn is worth. This is the mastery activity: your child turns the setup into symbols, then into a story, without help.

clicking.signs: Your child writes n + 5 for "some stickers and 5 more" without help. They can also turn 4 × n back into a story, like 4 friends who each have the same number of cards.
clicking.mixup: Writing 5 − n for "5 less than a number." The words come in that order, so this mistake makes sense.
clicking.todo: Test it with a real number. Ask, "If you had 10 stickers, what is 5 less?" Then put 10 in place of n in both n − 5 and 5 − n. Only one of them gives 5.
clicking.revisit: If the mix-up keeps coming back, spend a few days turning word problems into number sentences (Grade 4, Concept 10) before moving on.
